name: Hooke's law
anchor: OpenStax spring section: k as stiffness in N/m, the small-deformation limit where it stops being true, x measured from the relaxed position
variants: Stretch a spring and it pulls back. Go twice as far and it pulls twice as hard: F = -k*x. The minus sign means the pull always aims back toward the relaxed position. A big k is a stiff spring.
Every solid deforms a little under force, even a brick wall. For small pushes the deformation tracks the force exactly, and that is F = -k*x. Push far enough and it bends for good, and the law quits.
Here x is not the length of the spring, it is how far you dragged it off its rest position. F = -k*x is the force it spends undoing that. k is in N/m, so it reads as newtons per meter pulled.

name: net work of a heat engine per cycle
anchor: OpenStax heat engines: internal energy unchanged over a full cycle, the second law forbidding Q_c from being zero, and a car radiator
variants: An engine swallows heat Q_h, dumps some of it as Q_c, and keeps the gap as work: W = Q_h - Q_c. Nothing hides inside, because after a full cycle the engine sits exactly where it started.
You would love Q_c to be nothing and turn all the heat into work. The second law of thermodynamics says no. So every engine pays the cold side something, and W = Q_h - Q_c is what is left for you.
Burning fuel delivers Q_h, the exhaust and the coolant carry off Q_c, and only the gap between them turns the wheels: W = Q_h - Q_c. That is why a car needs a radiator.

name: momentum change from a velocity change
anchor: OpenStax impulse-momentum theorem: the tennis racquet and the goalie catching a puck, plus force acting over time
variants: Momentum is mass times velocity, so with the mass fixed only the velocity change counts: Delta_p = m*Delta_v. Velocity, not speed: a ball sent straight back has a big Delta_v even at the same speed.
A goalie catching a puck has to absorb all of its momentum. Delta_p = m*Delta_v says how much: double the mass, or double the change in speed, and the catch gets twice as hard to make.

Force times the time you apply it is what changes momentum, and Delta_p = m*Delta_v is that change. Stretch the time and the force drops for the same Delta_p, which is why braking early is gentler than late.

name: Energy of a photon
anchor: OpenStax photoelectric effect: Einstein's light quanta, energy set by frequency alone, one visible photon being a tiny fraction of a joule
variants: Light arrives in packets, and a packet's energy is set by its color alone: E_f = h*f. Brightness only counts how many turn up. Dim blue light can knock electrons loose where bright red light cannot.

Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by saying a light beam is a stream of particles, each one carrying E_f = h*f, where h is Planck's constant. Frequency fixes the energy. Nothing else about the beam does.

One photon of visible light carries a tiny sliver of a joule, which is why you never feel them land one by one. E_f = h*f, with f the frequency in Hz and h Planck's constant, is where that smallness comes from.

name: AC version of Ohm's law
anchor: OpenStax impedance section: Z combining R, X_L and X_C so they partly cancel rather than add, and resonance in a radio tuner
variants: Same shape as ordinary Ohm's law, with impedance Z standing in for resistance: I_0 = V_0/Z. The twist is that Z shifts with frequency, so one circuit can wave some tones through and choke others.

A radio tuner lives on this. I_0 = V_0/Z turns peak voltage into peak current, and at one frequency the coil and the capacitor cancel, Z drops to just the resistance, and that station comes through loud.
Coils and capacitors impede current in opposite ways, so they partly cancel and their ohms refuse to simply add. Whatever total Z falls out, the peak current follows from I_0 = V_0/Z.

name: electrical power from voltage and resistance
anchor: OpenStax power in electric circuits: bulbs of different wattage on the same fixed supply voltage, and electron collisions leaving as heat and light
variants: At a wall outlet the voltage is fixed, so the only thing setting how bright a bulb burns is its own resistance: P = V^2/R. Lower R, more power, hotter filament. That is the whole difference between bulbs.

Notice the square. Double the voltage across the same resistor and the power does not double, it goes up fourfold: P = V^2/R. A small mistake in voltage can cook a component that would have been fine.

The power is not lost, it is converted. Electrons bang into the metal and give up what they gained, and it leaves as heat and light. P = V^2/R is how much, every second, for voltage V across resistance R.

name: Optical power
anchor: OpenStax vision correction: diopters on a real glasses prescription, negative power for a diverging lens, and lens powers adding where focal lengths do not
variants: Your glasses prescription is this number. P = 1/f, with the focal length f written in meters, gives the optical power in diopters. A short focal length bends light hard, so it earns a big P.

A negative P means a diverging lens, thin in the middle, what a nearsighted person wears. Positive means converging and thick in the middle. Since P = 1/f, the sign comes straight off the focal length.
Opticians work in P = 1/f rather than f because the powers of lenses sitting close together simply add, while focal lengths do not. Your cornea and your eye lens team up exactly that way.

name: Approximate time for exchange of a virtual particle between two other particles
anchor: no evidence paragraphs supplied; written from the uncertainty principle and the short range of a force carried by a massive particle, with h declared by the record's own cval
variants: Quantum rules let a particle flicker into being with energy E so long as it disappears fast enough. Delta_t = h/E is that deadline, with h Planck's constant. Borrow more energy, get less time to repay it.

Forces are carried by particles nobody sees directly. A heavier carrier costs more energy E and so lives a shorter time: Delta_t = h/E. Short life means short reach, which is why some forces stop at the nucleus.
Here h is Planck's constant, and it is minuscule, so Delta_t = h/E comes out minuscule as well. Even a modest energy E buys the particle nothing more than the barest flicker before it has to vanish.

name: first law of thermodynamics
anchor: metabolism as energy bookkeeping, plus the chemistry-vs-physics sign flip on W from the req field
variants: Nothing is lost, only moved. Delta_U = Q - W says the heat Q you put in that does not leave as work W stays behind as internal energy. Watch the minus: W is work done BY the system, not on it.
Eat a burrito and your internal energy climbs; do work and it drops. That is Delta_U = Q - W, heat in minus work out, and the leftover is what you keep. It never asks how messy the middle was.

Chemists write this law with a plus and physicists with a minus, and both are right because they mean different W. Here W is work the system does, so it subtracts: Delta_U = Q - W. Check whose W you have.

name: energy-mass conversion
anchor: the sun turning a little mass into the light you feel, and electron-positron annihilation
variants: Mass is energy that is sitting still. E = m*c^2 is the exchange rate, and since c is the speed of light it is a brutal one: the sun loses a little mass and you feel it on your face.

Let an electron meet a positron and both stop existing, leaving light behind. Nothing was destroyed, only converted, and E = m*c^2 is the receipt: the mass that vanished fixes the energy that shows up.
Almost every bit of energy you have ever used traces back to mass disappearing somewhere. E = m*c^2 sets the rate, and squaring the speed of light makes it enormous, so a tiny m buys a huge E.

name: Displacement
anchor: the pacing professor who ends one step from where she began, and walking there and back
variants: Walk to the fridge and back and your displacement is zero, whatever your legs think. Delta_x = x_f - x_i only looks at the two endpoints, and the path you took between them appears nowhere in it.

Displacement has a direction, not just a size. Pick which way counts as positive first, then Delta_x = x_f - x_i comes out negative when you finish behind where you started. That minus is information.
A professor can pace all lecture and end one step left of the board. Delta_x = x_f - x_i counts that step and nothing else. Distance walked is a different number, and never the smaller of the two.

name: photon frequency from an energy-level difference
anchor: an electron falling between two levels and paying out one whole photon; line spectra as element fingerprints
variants: An electron drops from the L level to the K level and the leftover energy leaves as one photon. f = Delta_E_LK / h fixes its frequency: a wider gap buys a higher f, never a faster photon. h is Planck's constant.

Atoms glow in fixed colors because their levels sit at fixed heights. The gap Delta_E_LK between two of them sets the frequency exactly, f = Delta_E_LK / h, which is how you tell elements apart by light.
Light comes in whole photons, so a jump cannot pay out half of one. Divide the energy gap by Planck's constant, f = Delta_E_LK / h, and that jump can emit one frequency and no other.

name: length of a closed tube from its fundamental
anchor: blowing across a bottle, and the sealed end forcing exactly a quarter wave into the tube
variants: Blow across a bottle and the air inside picks one note. A tube closed at one end holds a quarter of a wave, so L = v_w / (4*f_1), and the longer the column the lower its fundamental f_1.
You can measure a pipe you cannot see into. Hear its lowest note f_1, know the speed of sound v_w, and L = v_w / (4*f_1) hands you the length, no ruler and nothing put inside the tube.
Air cannot move at the sealed end, so the wave has to be still there and swinging hardest at the mouth. That fits exactly a quarter wavelength, which is the 4 in L = v_w / (4*f_1).

name: Carnot efficiency
anchor: the heat you must dump to reset, and efficiency collapsing as the two reservoirs close together
variants: No engine beats this. Eff_C = 1 - (T_c/T_h) is a ceiling set by the two temperatures alone, not by how clever the machine is, and you only climb toward it by heating T_h or chilling T_c.

You never get all the heat as work, because the engine must dump some into the cold side to be ready for the next stroke. Eff_C = 1 - (T_c/T_h) is the most you could keep. Put both temperatures in kelvin.
Push the two reservoirs together and the whole thing collapses: as T_c creeps up toward T_h, Eff_C = 1 - (T_c/T_h) fades to nothing. Only a cold side at absolute zero would hand you everything.

name: Pressure
anchor: the same force through a thumbtack versus a palm; snowshoes; pressure on the nerve behind the eye
variants: Lean on a wall with your palm and nothing happens. Lean the same way on a thumbtack and it sinks in. Same force F, much smaller area A, and p = F/A is the entire difference between the two.

Force is what you apply; pressure is what the surface feels. Since p = F/A, shrinking the area is just another way of pushing harder. Snowshoes run it backwards: same weight, more A, and you stay on top.
In a fluid the pressure pushes on every surface it touches, and p = F/A turns it back into a force. Let the pressure in your eye build and that force on the nerve behind it is what does the damage.

name: Acceleration of center of mass of rolling object
anchor: the burnout, where the wheel spins and the car does not, because rolling contact has been lost
variants: A wheel that is not slipping cannot cheat. Its contact patch is momentarily at rest on the road, so spinning up harder drags the whole center along: a_CM = R*alpha, and a bigger R covers more road per turn.
The link breaks the moment the tire slips. In a burnout alpha is huge while a_CM is nearly nothing, the wheel spinning and the car going nowhere, so a_CM = R*alpha holds only while rubber grips road.
Spin and travel are two different motions, and rolling contact is what locks them together through the radius: a_CM = R*alpha. Give a big wheel and a small one the same alpha, the big one wins.

name: Motionally induced emf
variants: Slide a wire sideways through a magnetic field and a voltage shows up across its ends. That is epsilon = B*l*v: move faster, use a longer wire, or find a stronger field and you get more of it.
No battery anywhere. Motion alone shoves charge along a wire that cuts across a magnetic field, and epsilon = B*l*v says how much: field times length times speed. Stop moving and it dies at once.

The v is the catch. A wire sitting still in a magnetic field makes nothing, and one drifting along the field makes nothing either. It has to cut across. Then epsilon = B*l*v and your bike light glows.
anchor: generator / bike light; a still wire makes nothing

name: electron energy in the nth Bohr orbit
variants: An electron in an atom cannot sit just anywhere. Its energy is E_n = -E_0*(1/n^2), one rung per whole number n. The minus sign means bound: you have to pay energy to pull the electron loose.

Square the rung number and divide, that is the whole rule. E_n = -E_0*(1/n^2), so the low rungs sit far apart while the high ones crowd together near zero, where the electron stops belonging to the atom.

Starlight carries hydrogen's fingerprint. An electron falling from one n to a lower one dumps the gap as light, and E_n = -E_0*(1/n^2) fixes the rungs, so the same colors show up in a lamp and in a star.
anchor: rungs crowding toward zero; neon sign colors

name: Angular frequency of a mass-spring system in SHM
variants: Two things set the wobble rate and nothing else gets a vote. Stiffness speeds it up, mass drags it down, and omega = sqrt(k/m) is that tug of war. The root means mass has to grow a lot to slow it much.

Pull the mass further out and it still takes the same time to come back. Amplitude drops out of the answer completely. What is left is omega = sqrt(k/m), the spring's stiffness fighting the load's inertia.

Bounce a car on its suspension: a stiffer spring makes it quicker, a heavier load makes it slower. omega = sqrt(k/m) is that rate in radians per second, so it runs higher than the bounces you could count.
anchor: stiffness against inertia; amplitude drops out

name: Time constant
variants: Your camera flash takes ages to charge and empties in an instant. Same capacitor, different R. tau = R*C is the clock of the circuit: raise either the resistance or the capacitance and everything slows.

Multiply an ohm by a farad and you get a second, which is the surprise in it. tau = R*C is how long a capacitor takes to mostly fill or mostly empty. It never quite finishes, it just keeps closing in.

A lamp that blinks by itself is a capacitor filling until a neon tube breaks down and dumps it, over and over. tau = R*C sets the pace, so swapping the resistor or the capacitor changes the blink rate.
anchor: camera flash charges slow and dumps fast; blinking neon lamp

name: Frequency of a mass-spring system in SHM
variants: Pluck a guitar string gently or hard and the note does not change. Amplitude is nowhere in f = (1/(2*pi))*sqrt(k/m). Only the stiffness k and the mass m are, and nothing else gets a say.
Stiffen a diving board and it vibrates faster. Put a heavier person on it and it slows right down. That trade is f = (1/(2*pi))*sqrt(k/m), stiffness on top of the fraction, mass underneath.
The 2*pi is bookkeeping, turning radians per second into bounces per second. The physics is the ratio under the root in f = (1/(2*pi))*sqrt(k/m). Stiff and light is quick, floppy and heavy is slow.
anchor: guitar string plucked hard or gently; stiffer diving board

name: Capacitance
variants: Push charge onto a capacitor and the voltage climbs to match, so the ratio C = Q/V never budges. It tells you how much charge one volt buys, and that holds right up to the voltage where the gap arcs over.
Here is the odd part. C = Q/V, yet C does not depend on Q or on V. It is fixed by the plates, their spacing and whatever material sits between them. Charge and voltage just move together.

You cannot get a bigger C by charging harder. C = Q/V is decided by how the thing is built, so you shove the plates closer or slide an insulator between them, and then the same volts hold more charge.
anchor: C fixed by plates and spacing, not by charge; dielectric

name: gravitational acceleration from a pendulum period
variants: String, a weight, a stopwatch: that is a gravity meter. Time the swing, measure the length, and g = 4*pi^2*L/T^2 hands you gravity. The mass of the bob never appears, and that is not an oversight.
Run the pendulum period T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) backwards and gravity falls out of it. Because T sits squared underneath in g = 4*pi^2*L/T^2, sloppy timing costs you more than a sloppy ruler does.
Keep the swings narrow. Open the arc up wide and the period creeps longer, and g = 4*pi^2*L/T^2 quietly stops being true. Stay inside that small-swing limit and string can weigh a planet.
anchor: string and stopwatch as a gravimeter; small-swing limit

name: rms voltage
variants: An outlet's voltage swings up and down all day, so the peak V_0 is not the number anyone quotes. V_rms = V_0/sqrt(2) is the steady DC voltage that would heat the same toaster just as fast.

Average an AC voltage over a cycle and you get nothing, since it spends as long negative as positive. So you square it, average that, then take the root. For a sine wave it lands on V_rms = V_0/sqrt(2).
The number printed on the outlet is the rms one, not the top of the swing. V_rms = V_0/sqrt(2), so the real peak V_0 runs higher than the label, and the insulation has to survive that peak.
anchor: the wall outlet is quoted rms; average of AC is zero

name: average AC power from rms current and voltage
variants: An AC current swings both ways, so its plain average is zero. Root mean square is the fix: square it, average, take the root. Then P_ave = I_rms*V_rms, exactly like a DC circuit.
The volts printed on a wall socket are V_rms, not the peak the wire actually reaches. rms values are the DC equivalents, so power stays simple: P_ave = I_rms*V_rms.
AC power pulses as the current reverses, and nobody cares about the pulsing, only what is left after you average it. That is P_ave = I_rms*V_rms, the wattage on the back of a microwave.
anchor: OpenStax: rms values are the equivalent DC values, and ratings are quoted as rms, not peak

name: Index of refraction
variants: Light crawls through glass or water because it keeps bumping into atoms. n = c/v is just how much it slows: c in empty space over v in the stuff. Nothing beats c, so n is never below one.
n = c/v compares light's speed in vacuum to its speed inside a material. Air hardly slows it, so air sits near one. Water and glass slow it more, so their n is bigger.
Push a mower off the path onto grass: one wheel drags and it turns. Light bends the same way where v drops, and n = c/v measures the drop. n shifts with color, so a prism splits white light.
anchor: OpenStax: the lawn-mower-onto-grass analogy, n >= 1 always, n near 1 for gases, prism from wavelength shift

name: fundamental frequency of a closed tube
variants: Blow across a tube closed at one end and the longest wave that fits is four tube lengths: air is pinned still at the closed end, free at the open one. That lowest note is f_1 = v/(4*L).
f_1 = v/(4*L) is the lowest note a tube closed at one end can hold. Double the length L and the pitch drops an octave, which is why the long pipes on an organ are the low ones.
The v in f_1 = v/(4*L) is the speed of sound, and sound moves faster in warm air. So a closed pipe goes sharp as it warms, and players blow through a wind instrument to settle it first.
anchor: OpenStax: node at the closed end, fundamental has lambda = 4L, organs in cold cathedrals and warming instruments

name: Angular magnification M of a simple magnifier
variants: A magnifier makes nothing bigger. It makes things cover more of your view. M = theta_image/theta_object is the angle the image fills over the angle it filled before, and your eye reads that as size.
Hold your thumb at arm's length, then near your nose. Same thumb, wider angle, looks bigger. That is all magnifying is, and M = theta_image/theta_object is the angle you get over the angle you had.
M = theta_image/theta_object is one angle over another, so it carries no units at all. A magnifier earns a big M by letting you hold something right up to your eye and still see it sharp.
anchor: OpenStax: ratio of the angle subtended by the image to that subtended by the object; long objective, short eyepiece

name: power dissipated in a resistor
variants: Push current through a resistor and it warms up. P = I^2*R says how fast. The square is what bites: double the current and the heat quadruples. That is how a toaster wire gets to glowing.
Every resistor is a small heater. Energy leaves the circuit as heat at the rate P = I^2*R, and resistors in a row all carry the same current, so the one with the biggest R runs hottest.
P = I^2*R falls out of two rules you already have. Power is current times voltage, and Ohm's law turns that voltage into I times R. Multiply, and you are left with watts: joules every second.
anchor: OpenStax: Joule's law with Ohm's law substituted in; series resistors all carry the same full current

name: beat frequency from two waves that differ in frequency
variants: Play two notes almost in tune and the loudness throbs. They drift in and out of step, and f_beat = |f_2 - f_1| is how often. Nudge them closer and the throbbing slows right down.
A tuner does not listen for the right pitch, they listen for the beating to stop. f_beat = |f_2 - f_1| sets its rate, so slower beating means the two strings have got closer together.
f_beat = |f_2 - f_1| is the gap between two frequencies, and the bars mean take it positive: it makes no difference which tone is higher. When f_2 and f_1 meet, the beating dies away.
anchor: NO EVIDENCE AND NO GLOSSARY in the record; written from the physics of two tones drifting in and out of phase

name: mass from density and volume
variants: Density says how much mass is crammed into each cubic meter, so the mass is that times how many cubic meters you have: m = rho*V. Same size lump, bigger rho, heavier in your hand.
Archimedes could test a crown without melting it. Dunk it, read the volume V it pushes aside, and m = rho*V gives the mass a solid gold one that size would have. Mismatch, and the metal is wrong.
m = rho*V is rho = m/V rearranged, nothing more. V you can get by dunking the thing in water and watching the level. Multiply by the density of whatever it is made of and the mass drops out.
anchor: OpenStax: the king of Syracuse's crown, and the silver coin whose volume is found by water displacement

name: Absolute pressure
variants: A flat tire still has air in it. The gauge reads zero because it only counts what is above the air around it, and p_abs = p_g + p_atm adds that air back to give the real pressure.
A gauge starts counting from the atmosphere it sits in, not from nothing. p_abs = p_g + p_atm puts the atmosphere back on. Pump a vacuum chamber and p_g goes negative while p_abs stays positive.
p_g is what your gauge shows, p_atm is the air already pressing on everything, and p_abs = p_g + p_atm is the total. Fluids push and never pull, so p_abs cannot drop below zero, though p_g can.
anchor: OpenStax: a tire gauge reads only above atmospheric, a vacuum chamber gauge reads negative, fluids push so p_abs >= 0

name: photon wavelength from energy
anchor: Compton's X-ray scattering; a single visible photon too faint to sense
variants: Ask a photon how much energy it carries and you have asked its wavelength too: lambda = (h*c)/E locks the two together. Violet carries more energy per photon than red, so violet's wave is the shorter one.

Give a photon more energy and its wave gets shorter, not taller. lambda = (h*c)/E. X-rays sit way up at the energy end, so their wavelength is tiny, which is how Compton caught them knocking electrons loose.

Light has no mass you can weigh, so you size a photon by its energy instead. lambda = (h*c)/E converts one to the other. Planck's constant h is so small that a single photon of light is far too faint to feel.

name: mass from net force and acceleration
anchor: OpenStax basketball vs car under the same net external force
variants: Mass is really just how stubborn something is. Push with a known force, watch how fast it picks up speed, divide: m = F_net/a. Shove a basketball and a car equally hard and the car barely notices.
Mass here gets measured, not looked up. The same force gives a light thing a big acceleration and a heavy thing a small one, so m = F_net/a reads the mass straight off that difference.

Newton's second law, turned around to hand you the mass. m = F_net/a, and net is the word that bites: add up every force on the thing, with friction pulling the other way. Miss one and the mass comes out wrong.

name: energy stored in a capacitor
anchor: OpenStax defibrillator and camera flash; average voltage is V/2 while charging
variants: A capacitor starts empty, so the first charge slips in free and the last one fights full voltage. Average those and you get the half: U_E = (1/2)*C*V^2. Double the voltage and you store four times as much.
A defibrillator dumps this into a chest and a camera flash burns it in a blink. U_E = (1/2)*C*V^2, so cranking the voltage buys far more energy than fitting a bigger capacitor does.
Charge two plates and the energy is not sitting on the charge, it is out in the field between them. U_E = (1/2)*C*V^2. Cut the battery away and the plates keep it until you let a bulb drain them.

name: Newton's second law, scalar form
anchor: OpenStax: net EXTERNAL force, and the law rests on experiment not derivation
variants: Nothing speeds up, slows down or turns on its own. Something has to push it. F_net = m*a sizes that push, and net is the catch: it is every force added together, friction included, not just yours.

Acceleration is not only going faster. Braking counts. So does rounding a corner at steady speed. Each one leaves the acceleration nonzero, so F_net = m*a says a force is acting even if you cannot see what.

Nobody derived F_net = m*a on paper. It is a claim about the world that experiments kept agreeing with, which is what makes it a law. Scalar form means you want how big the force is, not where it points.

name: Tangential speed
anchor: OpenStax CD and car tire: same omega, larger r, larger speed
variants: Stand on the equator and Earth's spin carries you along quickly; stand near a pole and it hardly moves you, though the whole planet turns together. v_t = r*omega, and r is your distance from the axis.
Fit bigger wheels and the car covers more ground per turn of the axle. v_t = r*omega: omega is how fast the wheel spins, r is its radius, and the product is how fast the car actually travels.
Everyone on a merry-go-round sweeps the same angle, but the rider on the outside covers a longer arc doing it. v_t = r*omega is that sentence in symbols. Same omega, bigger r, more meters per second.

name: horizontal displacement in projectile motion
anchor: OpenStax fireworks shell; sideways acceleration is zero when air is negligible
variants: Sideways, nothing is pushing a thrown ball, so it keeps whatever sideways speed you gave it. x = v_0x*t is just distance equals speed times time. Gravity is busy with the vertical part and leaves this alone.
Drop one ball and fire another sideways at the same instant and they land together. The sideways motion does not care what gravity is doing: x = v_0x*t, steady speed for the whole flight.
Air resistance is what breaks this one. Ignore the air and v_0x never changes, so x = v_0x*t. Throw a beach ball instead of a stone and the air eats the sideways speed and it lands well short.

name: acceleration of two blocks connected over a pulley
anchor: OpenStax two attached blocks: m_1 on a frictionless table, m_2 hanging on a string
variants: Gravity pulls on both blocks, but the table holds m_1 up, so only the hanging block's weight is left to pull, and the string drags m_1 along anyway. a = (m_2/(m_1+m_2))*g, one weight moving two masses.
The pair always falls slower than a free drop, because m_2/(m_1+m_2) is less than one. a = (m_2/(m_1+m_2))*g. Pile mass onto m_1 and it barely creeps; take m_1 away and you are back to plain g.
Pull comes from one block, inertia comes from both, and a = (m_2/(m_1+m_2))*g splits the difference. It assumes a frictionless table and a weightless pulley, so a real bench setup runs slower.

name: Molar heat capacity at constant pressure
anchor: no evidence paragraphs supplied; glossary only restates constant pressure
variants: Heat a gas in a sealed box and every joule goes into the gas. Let it expand at steady pressure and some of it goes into shoving the atmosphere out of the way, so you need more: C_p = C_V + R.
The gap between the two heat capacities is exactly R, the gas constant. C_p = C_V + R, because at constant pressure a mole of gas does R worth of work per degree just making room for itself.
Water in a pan hardly swells when you heat it, so its two heat capacities are nearly the same. A gas has to shove the air back to make room, and for a mole that costs R per degree: C_p = C_V + R.

name: arc length
anchor: OpenStax CD pits: same angle swept, different ground covered
variants: Two dots on a spinning CD sweep the same angle, but the outer one covers far more ground. The distance it actually travels is s = r*theta. Double the radius and you double the arc.
Arc length is ordinary distance, only measured along a curve. s = r*theta is how you get it: the radius is what turns an angle into meters. Go all the way around and s is the circumference.
An angle on its own tells you nothing about how far anything traveled. Multiply it by the radius and now it does: s = r*theta. That is also why theta carries no unit, and s comes out in meters.

name: Acceleration of an object rolling without slipping
anchor: OpenStax: rolling is slower than a frictionless slide, and depends on I_CM
variants: Race a can down a ramp against a block sliding with no friction, and the can loses. Some of the pull goes into spinning it up instead. a_CM = ((m*g*sin(theta))/(m+(I_CM/r^2))), and I_CM is the tax.
Look at the bottom of a_CM = ((m*g*sin(theta))/(m+(I_CM/r^2))). That I_CM/(r)^(2) acts like extra mass the slope has to shift, so mass parked out at the rim costs you the most.
Two cans of the same mass, same ramp, and the hollow one comes last every time. That is all I_CM: a_CM = ((m*g*sin(theta))/(m+(I_CM/r^2))). If it ever slips instead of rolling, throw this out.

name: Molar heat capacity at constant volume for an ideal gas with d degrees of freedom
anchor: OpenStax degrees of freedom: energy splits equally over each independent motion
variants: Heat gets split evenly over every independent way a molecule can move, and d counts those ways. Each one is worth half of R, so C_V = (d/2)*R. More ways to move, more heat per degree.
Why does one gas warm up faster than another, mole for mole, on the same burner? Its molecules have fewer places to put the energy. That count is d, and C_V = (d/2)*R turns it into heat capacity.
C_V = (d/2)*R holds the volume fixed on purpose. Let the gas expand instead and some of your heat leaves as work on the surroundings, and the number you need goes up.

name: Intensity at a second distance as a spherical wave expands
anchor: no evidence paragraphs supplied; written from inverse-square spreading over a sphere
variants: Step twice as far from a lamp and it is a quarter as bright, not half. The light is spread over a sphere, and a sphere's area grows with the square of its radius: I_2 = I_1*(r_1/r_2)^2.
Nothing is lost as the wave travels out. The same power just thins across a bigger and bigger shell: I_2 = I_1*(r_1/r_2)^2. Back away and the drop is brutal, since it is squared.
I_2 = I_1*(r_1/r_2)^2 assumes the source throws energy out in every direction. A laser barely spreads, so it holds up far better than this. A room full of echoes breaks it too.

name: Magnitude of magnetic force
anchor: OpenStax Magnetic Force: theta sits between v and B, and the force stays perpendicular to v
variants: A charge sitting still feels nothing from a magnet. Get it moving across the field and it does: F = q*v*B*sin(theta), where theta is the angle between v and B. Line v up with B and it dies.

This force always shoves sideways, square to wherever the charge is headed, so it bends the path instead of speeding the charge up. F = q*v*B*sin(theta). Curl your right fingers from v to B; your thumb is F.
Everything in F = q*v*B*sin(theta) has to show up at once: some charge q, some motion v, a field B, and an angle between the last two. Knock out any one of them and you are left with nothing.

name: Velocity of center of mass of rolling object
anchor: no evidence paragraphs supplied; written from the no-slip contact point being instantaneously at rest
variants: Roll a wheel without letting it skid and the bottom of it is, for that instant, not moving at all. That pins the middle to v_CM = R*omega. Same spin, bigger wheel, more ground covered.
v_CM = R*omega is less a formula than the definition of not slipping. Spin your tires on ice and the car crawls along slower than R*omega. Lock the brakes and it slides along faster.

One full turn of a wheel carries it forward by exactly one circumference, which locks spin rate to forward speed: v_CM = R*omega. Fit bigger tires and the speedometer reads low, since it only counts turns.

name: Binding energy
anchor: OpenStax mass defect: the nucleus weighs less than its nucleons, and the curve peaks at iron
variants: Weigh a nucleus, then weigh its protons and neutrons separately, and the loose parts come out heavier. That missing mass is Delta_m, and E = Delta_m*c^2 is the energy holding the thing together.
c is the speed of light, so squaring it turns a Delta_m far too small to weigh into a huge E = Delta_m*c^2. Coal fires shed mass the same way, just far too little for anyone to measure.
Nothing is bound tighter than iron, which is where fusion inside a star finally gives up. E = Delta_m*c^2 is the bill for pulling a nucleus apart, and Delta_m is the mass it was short.

name: Angle of rotation
anchor: OpenStax clock hand: hand length cancels out, which is what defines the radian
variants: Take how far you moved along the curve and divide by how far out you were: Delta_theta = (Delta_s/r). Both are meters, so they cancel and the angle is a bare number. That is what a radian is.
A long clock hand and a stubby one sweep the same angle from noon to three, but the long tip travels much further. Delta_theta = (Delta_s/r) divides that hand length straight back out.
Measure the angle this way and you get radians, never degrees. Delta_theta = (Delta_s/r), so going once around makes Delta_s the whole circumference. Use degrees in a later formula and it breaks.

name: Potential-energy function of a harmonic oscillator
anchor: marble settling in a bowl; turning points; the lopsided Lennard-Jones bond well
variants: Picture a marble in a bowl. It settles at the bottom, where x is zero, and climbing the sides costs energy. U = (1/2)*m*omega^2*x^2 is that bowl: go twice as far out, store four times as much.
Stretch an oscillator and the energy has to sit somewhere. It sits here, U = (1/2)*m*omega^2*x^2. At the turning point the mass stops dead and every bit of its motion is parked in this term.
Two atoms in a bond sit in an energy well and jiggle near the bottom. Down there the well looks like U = (1/2)*m*omega^2*x^2. Pull them far out and the real well goes lopsided and this stops working.

name: Intensity for a spherical wave
anchor: speaker on a post getting quieter as the sphere's area 4*pi*r^2 grows with r
variants: Walk away from a speaker and it gets quieter, but no sound went missing. The same power P is smeared over a bigger sphere, and a sphere has area 4*pi*r^2. So I = P/(4*pi*r^2).
Stand twice as far from a source and it hits you a quarter as hard. That is I = P/(4*pi*r^2). The power never changed; the sphere carrying it has four times the area, so it is thinner everywhere.
Energy leaving a source spreads over a growing sphere, so I = P/(4*pi*r^2) with r your distance out. It assumes nothing soaks up the wave on the way and the source radiates evenly in all directions.

name: Intensity of sound
anchor: pressure amplitude in air; rho and v are the medium; the ear's range is why decibels exist
variants: Sound is air being squeezed and let go. Delta_p_max is the hardest squeeze in the wave, and doubling it makes the sound four times as intense, not twice: I = (Delta_p_max)^2/(2*rho*v).
A microphone feels pressure, not power, and this turns one into the other: I = (Delta_p_max)^2/(2*rho*v). The rho and v are the air itself, so the same squeeze carries differently under water.
Your ear spans a brutal range of intensities, which is why we quote decibels instead. Underneath the decibels sits this: I = (Delta_p_max)^2/(2*rho*v), the pressure swing and the air it travels in.

name: rms current
anchor: AC's plain average is zero; rms is the equivalent DC value; breakers and nameplates quote rms
variants: AC current swings both ways, so its plain average is zero and tells you nothing. Square it, average that, take the root: I_rms = I_0/sqrt(2). It is the steady DC current that would heat the same.
A breaker trips on I_rms, not on the peak, and the peak is always the larger one: I_rms = I_0/sqrt(2). The current on an AC nameplate is rms too, so the real current does swing past that number.
Root two is not a law of nature. It is just what a smooth sine wave gives you: I_rms = I_0/sqrt(2). Square off that wave instead and the rms comes out equal to the peak, with no factor at all.

name: Tangential acceleration
anchor: Ferris wheel riders: same alpha, but rim and hub get different pushes
variants: A Ferris wheel starting up shoves you along your seat. How hard depends on how far out you sit: a_t = r*alpha. Build a smaller wheel, spin it up just as hard, and the riders get the gentler push.
Two accelerations act on you in a turn. a_t = r*alpha is the one that speeds you up along your path, not the one hauling you inward. Spin at a steady rate and alpha is zero, so a_t vanishes.
Turn the axle faster and a point out at radius r must cover more arc in the same time, so it has to accelerate harder to keep up. That is all a_t = r*alpha says. Double r and you double the push.

name: momentum of a photon (deBroglie relation)
anchor: comet tails always point away from the Sun; Compton's x-rays recoiling off electrons
variants: A comet's dust tail points away from the Sun, never behind the comet. Sunlight is shoving it. Light carries momentum with no mass at all, and p = h/lambda says shorter wavelength means a harder shove.
Compton fired x-rays at electrons and the x-rays came back with less energy, recoiling like billiard balls. That works only if a photon has momentum, and it does: p = h/lambda, h = 6.626e-34 J*s.
Momentum usually means mass times velocity, and a photon has no mass, so that road is closed. Use its wavelength instead: p = h/lambda. Blue light hits harder per photon than red for that reason.

name: Velocity
anchor: the velocity-vs-time graph: slope is a, intercept is v_0; velocity carries direction
variants: Draw velocity against time and a steady acceleration gives a straight line. Its slope is a, where it starts is v_0, so v = v_0 + a*t. You begin with some speed and add a bit more each second.
Acceleration is how much velocity you pick up each second, so holding it for t seconds adds a*t to whatever you had: v = v_0 + a*t. Braking is the same line with a negative a, sloping down.

Velocity now is velocity then plus whatever the acceleration added: v = v_0 + a*t. Two catches: a has to hold steady the whole time, and v_0 and a each carry a sign, so a can point against the motion.

name: angular velocity from tangential speed
anchor: spinning CD, rim travels further than centre for one shared omega; tire spinning on ice
variants: On a spinning CD every point finishes a turn together, so they share one omega, but the outer edge travels much further to do it. Divide that speed by how far out you are: omega = v/r.
A rolling tire turns spin into speed. Bigger tire at the same omega covers more road. Read it the other way and omega = v/r hands you how fast the wheel spins from how fast the car is going.

Spin rate is rim speed shared out over the radius: omega = v/r. The same speed closer in to the axis means a faster spin. Careful on ice, though: a tire can have a big omega while the car barely moves.

name: Acceleration
anchor: OpenStax: braking is still acceleration, and a constant-speed turn accelerates
variants: Acceleration is just how fast your velocity is changing: a = Delta_v/Delta_t. Hit the brakes and a points backward, against your motion. Physics still calls that acceleration, not its own thing.
Round a corner at a steady speed and you are still accelerating. Velocity carries a direction, so turning hands you a Delta_v even at a fixed speed, and a = Delta_v/Delta_t follows it.
Acceleration is velocity gained per second, nothing more: a = Delta_v/Delta_t. The unit m/s^2 reads exactly that way, meters per second, per second. A big Delta_v in a small Delta_t is a hard shove.

name: Law of refraction (Snell's law)
anchor: OpenStax: pencil bent in a glass, Ibn Sahl before Snell, one fish seen twice
variants: Stand a pencil in a glass of water and it looks snapped in two. Light kinks when it changes speed, and theta_2 = asin((n_1*sin(theta_1))/n_2) says by how much. Raise n_2 and the ray tips toward the perpendicular.

Snell got his name on it, but Ibn Sahl had the rule centuries earlier, working on burning mirrors and lenses. theta_2 = asin((n_1*sin(theta_1))/n_2): the indices and theta_1 together fix where the ray goes.

Look into a fish tank and one fish can seem to sit in two places. Rays bend as they leave the water, and theta_2 = asin((n_1*sin(theta_1))/n_2) tracks that bend from theta_1 and the indices on each side.

name: spring constant from force and extension
anchor: no usable evidence (one tier-words score-1 paragraph, about elastic PE); measuring k from a hung load
variants: k is stiffness boiled down to one number. Hang a force on a spring, measure the stretch, divide: k = F/x. Its unit N/m reads exactly that way, newtons per meter of stretch.
Two springs, same pull, different stretch? The one that moves less has the bigger k. That is the whole of k = F/x: force per unit of extension. Stiff means a lot of F buys you very little x.

You do not look k up, you measure it. Pull with F, note the extension x, take k = F/x. Stretch further and you should get the same k back. If you do not, you have pulled the spring past where it recovers.

name: energy of the nth level of a particle in a box
anchor: no evidence, no glossary; standing waves in a box, rungs spreading as the square
variants: Trap a particle between two walls and only certain standing waves fit, so its energy comes in rungs: K = n^2*E_1. E_1 is the bottom rung and n counts which one you are on. Nothing in between is allowed.
A guitar string sings only certain notes because both ends are pinned. A boxed particle is the same story. K = n^2*E_1 numbers the allowed modes, with E_1 setting the size of the lowest one.

K = n^2*E_1 says the ladder is not evenly spaced: double n and the energy goes up fourfold, so the rungs spread out as you climb. The particle cannot rest at the floor either; E_1 is already above it.

name: Angular momentum of a rotating rigid body
anchor: OpenStax: twin of linear momentum, right-hand rule, flywheels and planets (skater anchor is standard physics, not in the evidence)
variants: Spin is momentum with a pivot. L = I*omega is the rotational twin of mass times velocity: I is mass counted by how far it sits from the axis, omega how fast it turns. A flywheel holds its mass out at the rim.
Pull your arms in on a spinning stool and you speed up. L = I*omega does not change, so shrinking I has to raise omega. Hauling mass toward the axis is the whole trick, and skaters know it.

L = I*omega points along the axis, not along any moving piece of the body. Curl your right hand the way it turns and your thumb shows you where L aims. Planets carry it from spinning and from orbiting.

name: power from force and velocity
anchor: no evidence, no glossary; a car running out of force near top speed at fixed P
variants: Power is not force, it is force kept up at speed. P = F*v: push twice as hard at the same pace, or push the same at twice the pace, and either way you are working twice as fast.
Here is why a car quits accelerating near top speed. The engine holds P about fixed, so P = F*v leaves less and less F as v climbs, until what is left only just balances the drag.
P = F*v is work per second with the clock hidden inside v, which is already meters per second. Shove a wall and nothing moves: no v, so no P, however hard you strain.

name: Quality factor of a circuit
anchor: no evidence, no glossary; resonance width, a struck bell versus a thud
variants: Q says how picky a resonant circuit is. Q = omega_0/Delta_omega sets where it peaks against how wide the peak is, so a narrow Delta_omega gives a big Q and a tuner that hears one station, not its neighbors.
A struck bell is high Q, a thud is low Q. Q = omega_0/Delta_omega measures it: losses widen Delta_omega and blur the peak, so the more a circuit dumps into heat, the smaller its Q.
Two frequencies divided, so the units cancel and Q is a bare number. Q = omega_0/Delta_omega is the resonance over its width. High Q keeps ringing after you stop driving it; low Q dies out fast.

name: Intensity
anchor: OpenStax glossary power per unit area, plus the ear's range quoted in decibels
variants: Same power, spread thinner. I = P/A is watts divided by the area they land on, which is why a lens can scorch paper without adding any energy at all. It only shrinks A, and I climbs.
Walk away from a speaker and it goes quiet even though the speaker is doing the same work. The sound is spread over a bigger A, so I = P/A drops. Intensity is power per square meter, W/m^2.
Your ear spans an absurd range of I, whisper to jet engine, which is why sound gets quoted in decibels instead of raw numbers. Underneath the scale it is just I = P/A, power landing per square meter.

name: velocity in free fall, upward positive
variants: Toss a ball straight up and gravity takes the same bite out of its velocity every second, climbing or falling. That is v = v_0 - g*t, and g is how big the bite is. Up counts as positive, so it subtracts.
Gravity does not care which way you are moving. v = v_0 - g*t runs straight through the top of the arc, where v passes through zero and turns negative on the way down. One line, whole flight.
Free fall means nothing is touching the ball, not even air. Only then does v = v_0 - g*t hold. The instant it hits the ground its acceleration is no longer g and the line stops being true.
anchor: ball tossed up; sign of g; free fall ends at contact

name: output work
variants: Output work is what a machine hands you: the force it puts out times how far that force pushes. W_o = F_o*d_o. The d_o is how far the load moves, not how far you moved your hand, and the two are rarely equal.
Shove a lever a long way with a small force and the far end moves a short way with a big one. What comes out the other side is W_o = F_o*d_o, and friction keeps it under what you put in.
W_o = F_o*d_o is the useful work leaving a machine, output force times the distance it acts through. Divide it by the work you fed in and you have the machine's efficiency, always under one.
anchor: crowbar and lever trading force for distance; efficiency

name: total mass from rocket and propellant
variants: Weigh a loaded rocket and you get two things at once: the rocket itself and the propellant still in its tanks. m = m_R + m_g. Burn fuel and m_g falls, so m keeps shrinking as it climbs.
m = m_R + m_g splits a rocket into the part that stays, m_R, and the part it throws away, m_g. The split matters because only the thrown part is what shoves the rocket forward.
On the pad, most of a rocket is fuel and not rocket. m = m_R + m_g names both halves, and it is a snapshot: at liftoff m_g dominates, at burnout it is gone and m is just m_R.
anchor: rocket on the pad is mostly fuel; mass falls as it burns

name: Angular position
variants: Walk along a curve of radius r and cover arc length s. The angle you swept is theta = s/r. That is what a radian is, and since it is a length over a length, theta has no units at all.
One radian is the angle whose arc is exactly as long as the radius. theta = s/r counts how many of those you have turned through, so a wider circle needs a longer arc for the same theta.
theta = s/r is why a point at the rim of a spinning wheel and a point near the hub share one angle but not one distance. Same theta, bigger r, longer arc s. The angle is what they have in common.
anchor: radian as arc over radius; rim and hub of a spinning wheel

name: lens/mirror equation (solved version)
variants: Set an object at d_o, find where its image lands at d_i, and the optics tell you their own focal length: f = (d_i*d_o)/(d_o+d_i). It is the lens/mirror equation rearranged to hand you f.

Signs do the real work here. A convex security mirror puts the image behind the glass and closer in than you are, so d_i is negative but d_o+d_i stays positive, and f = (d_i*d_o)/(d_o+d_i) comes out negative.
One relation covers lenses and curved mirrors both. f = (d_i*d_o)/(d_o+d_i) turns two measured distances into a focal length, and it only holds for rays that stay close to the axis.
anchor: virtual image behind a convex mirror makes d_i and f negative

name: Focal length for a spherical mirror
variants: A spherical mirror is a slice off a sphere of radius R, and parallel light crosses the axis halfway to that sphere's center. f = R/2. Flatten the mirror, R grows, and the focus runs away with it.
f = R/2 is an approximation, not a law. It holds for rays that stay near the axis; rays far off-axis miss the focus, which is why a serious telescope uses a parabola and not a sphere.
You need one measurement to find a spherical mirror's focus. Measure the curvature radius R, halve it, that is f. A tightly curved shaving mirror has small R, so its focus sits close in.
anchor: focus halfway to the sphere's center; parabola beats sphere off-axis

name: force from rate of momentum change
variants: Force is about how fast momentum changes: F = (m*Delta_v)/(Delta_t). Same mass, same change in speed, but spread over a longer Delta_t and F drops. That is the entire job of an airbag.
A racquet does not change a ball's speed instantly, it needs contact time. F = (m*Delta_v)/(Delta_t) gives the average force over that contact, so a short, sharp hit means an enormous F.
F = (m*Delta_v)/(Delta_t) assumes m holds still while the velocity changes. With m fixed out front it is just Newton's second law. For something shedding mass, like a rocket, do not use it.
anchor: airbag stretching Delta_t; racquet contact time; constant-mass caveat

name: quantum number from energy, particle in a box
variants: Trap a particle in a box and its energy can only sit on rungs, each one n^2 times the lowest. Read that backwards and n = (K/E_1)^(1/2) tells you which rung an energy K is sitting on.
n = (K/E_1)^(1/2) counts levels, not energy. The rungs climb as n^2, so they spread further apart the higher you go, and it takes a big jump in K to move n up by even one.
Every energy the box allows is E_1 times a perfect square, so n = (K/E_1)^(1/2) has to come out a whole number. If it lands between two of them, the box has no level at that K.
anchor: energy rungs in a box climbing as n^2 above E_1

name: wave speed from wavelength and period
variants: A wave moves forward exactly one wavelength every period. That is all v = lambda/T says. Watch a gull on the swell: it bobs once while the crest under it slides to where the next crest was.
Crest to crest is lambda. Crest to crest in time is T. Divide and you have how fast the shape travels, v = lambda/T. The water itself goes almost nowhere; only the pattern moves along.
v = lambda/T holds for ripples, sound and light alike. Hold v steady and a shorter lambda just means crests arriving sooner. How tall the wave is never enters into it.
anchor: seagull bobbing once on an ocean swell

name: de Broglie wavelength from mass and speed
variants: Anything with momentum also behaves like a wave, and lambda = h/(m*v) is how long that wave is. Momentum sits on the bottom, so heavy or fast means short. You have one. It is hopelessly small.
Divide h by momentum m*v and what comes out is a length. That length is how smeared out the thing acts: lambda = h/(m*v). Slow an electron down and its wave grows until crystals can diffract it.
de Broglie guessed that matter ripples the way light does. lambda = h/(m*v) says nothing big is ever wavy, because h is minute and momentum is not. Shrink m*v and the wave side shows up.
anchor: a slowed electron until crystals diffract it

name: Entropy change of a system in a reversible isothermal process
variants: Pour heat into something and its disorder rises by Delta_S = Q/T. The same joule buys more of it in a cold body than a hot one, which is why heat drifts from hot to cold. T is in kelvin.
Entropy is bookkeeping for how spread out energy is. Move Q in at a steady T and the ledger shifts by Q/T. Take heat out and Q goes negative, so that body's entropy falls while the other climbs.
Delta_S = Q/T needs two things: the temperature must not budge while the heat moves, and it must move slowly enough to run backward. Rush it and the real entropy change comes out bigger.
anchor: the same joule buys more disorder when cold

name: Displacement of center of mass of rolling object
variants: Roll a wheel without letting it skid and the tread it lays down is exactly how far the axle traveled: d_CM = R*theta. Chalk the rim and the floor marks sit one full circumference apart.
theta has to be in radians here, because R*theta is arc length, the strip of rim that actually touched the ground. Spin the wheel on ice and it turns while going nowhere, and d_CM = R*theta dies.
The middle of a rolling body keeps pace with the rim unwinding beneath it, so d_CM = R*theta. Same turn on a bigger R covers more ground, which is why wheel size is worth arguing about.
anchor: chalk mark on a rolling rim, and ice

name: Relativistic Doppler effect for frequency
variants: Light from something running away arrives lower in frequency. f_obs = f_s*sqrt((1-v/c)/(1+v/c)), and v counts positive for receding, so the bracquet drops under one and the color slides red.
An ambulance siren drops as it passes, and light does the same. c is the same for everyone, but the frequency and the wavelength both shift: f_obs = f_s*sqrt((1-v/c)/(1+v/c)). Negative v means blue.
Astronomers run this backward. A known line arrives shifted, and f_obs = f_s*sqrt((1-v/c)/(1+v/c)) hands back v. The far galaxies all come out red, all running away from us.
anchor: red-shifted galaxies running away from us

name: Rotational power
variants: It is the straight-line power rule turned sideways: swap the push for a twist and the speed for a spin rate, and you get P = tau*omega. Hold the power fixed and you trade one for the other.
P = tau*omega is how you get shaft torque out of an engine rating. You know the watts, you know the revs, the twist falls out. Gearing only trades them: at the wheels, big tau comes with small omega.
Twist harder or spin faster and either way you deliver more power: P = tau*omega. Keep omega in radians per second. The radian is a bare ratio, so it never shows up in the units.
anchor: engine gearing, torque traded against revs

name: velocity from constant acceleration starting at rest
variants: Acceleration is how much speed you pick up each second, so after t seconds of a steady a you have picked up a*t. Start from rest and that gain is the whole speed: v = a*t. A dragster is this.
v = a*t has rest baked into it. It is the full rule with the starting speed set to zero, so the moment the clock starts while you are already rolling, it is wrong and you must add what you had.
Plot speed against time a*t constant a and you get a straight line out of the origin with slope a. Read any point off it and that is v = a*t. Let a wander during the run and the line bends.
anchor: a dragster leaving the line from rest

name: apparent depth of an object seen through a flat refracting surface
variants: A coin on the pool floor looks nearer the surface than it is. s_i = (n_2/n_1)*s_o, with n_1 the stuff the coin sits in and n_2 the stuff your eye is in. Water under air, and it rises.
Light bends on its way out of the water, so your eye traces it back to the wrong place. That mistake is s_i = (n_2/n_1)*s_o. Spearing a fish means aiming under where you can see it.

Depth is the only thing that changes here. A flat surface magnifies nothing sideways, so the fish keeps its true width and just sits too shallow: s_i = (n_2/n_1)*s_o, measured straight down, not across.
anchor: coin on a pool floor; spearing a fish

name: Relationship between frequency and period
anchor: paycheck twice a month; waves per second vs seconds per wave
variants: Count how many waves go past each second and you have f. Time one single wave and you have T. Same fact, flipped over: f = 1/T. Double how often it repeats and the period is cut in half.
Get paid twice a month and your pay frequency is two per month, or the period between checks is half a month. Waves work the same way, f = 1/T. Hz just means cycles per second.
A plucked guitar string repeats the same trip over and over. T is how long one trip takes, f is how many trips per second, and f = 1/T ties them. Halve T and you double f.

name: Path length difference for waves from two slits to a common point on a screen
anchor: one slit is farther from the spot than the other
variants: Light from two slits lands on the same spot, but one path was slightly longer. That extra travel is Delta_l = d*sin(theta). Straight ahead theta is zero, the paths tie, and the waves arrive in step.
Delta_l = d*sin(theta) is how much farther the light from one slit had to go. If that extra distance is a whole number of wavelengths the waves add up; half a wavelength off and they cancel.
Look off to the side and one slit is now farther from you than the other. The gap is d*sin(theta), and every bright and dark band in a double slit comes from it. Needs a far away screen.

name: horizontal position under constant velocity
anchor: projectile coasting sideways; the one evidence paragraph is about vertical free fall and never teaches this relation
variants: Nothing pushes it sideways, so it just keeps going. Start at x_0, add v_x for every second that passes: x = x_0 + v_x*t. This is the horizontal half of a projectile, coasting the whole flight.
Roll a ball across a smooth floor and it covers the same distance each second. That is x = x_0 + v_x*t. There is no acceleration term because constant velocity means v_x is not changing.
x_0 is where you started, v_x*t is how far you have coasted since, so add them for where you are now. The moment friction or a push changes v_x, x = x_0 + v_x*t stops being true.

name: Angular velocity from constant angular acceleration
anchor: merry-go-round, CD slowing to a halt, fishing reel
variants: Push a merry-go-round at a steady rate and its spin climbs at a steady rate. omega_f = omega_0 + alpha*t. Take the spin it already had, then add alpha for every second you keep pushing.
Switch off a CD player and the disk slows smoothly to a stop. That is alpha with a minus sign, eating into omega_0 until nothing is left: omega_f = omega_0 + alpha*t. Only true if alpha holds steady.
A fish runs and the reel spins up. alpha is how fast the spin rate itself changes, so alpha*t is the spin gained in time t, and omega_f = omega_0 + alpha*t adds it to what you started with.

name: Law of reflection
anchor: angles measured from the normal; mirrors beat lenses in telescopes
variants: Light leaves a mirror at the same angle it arrived, theta_r = theta_i. The catch is where you measure from: not the surface, but the line perpendicular to it. Miss that and the whole problem tilts.

Whatever angle light hits a mirror at, it leaves at the same one: theta_r = theta_i. That holds for every color, which is why big telescopes use mirrors. A lens bends blue more than red and smears the image.
Squint at sunlight glinting off a lake and you are watching theta_r = theta_i. Angle in equals angle out, measured from the normal, so the glare reaches you from just one strip of water.

name: Wavelength in a medium of refractive index n
anchor: frequency is unchanged across a boundary, so the wave bunches up
variants: Light entering glass slows down but still arrives just as often, so the waves have to bunch up. lambda_n = lambda/n is that squeezed wavelength inside, where lambda is the vacuum value.
n says how much a medium slows light, and the wavelength shrinks by the same factor: lambda_n = lambda/n. A red laser stays red underwater, because color follows frequency and frequency is untouched.
Same wave, tighter spacing. In a medium of index n the wavelength is lambda/n, shorter than it was in vacuum. Bigger n, bigger squeeze. Send it back out to air and it stretches right back.

name: normal force on an object on an inclined plane
anchor: a surface can only push straight out of itself; weight split by coordinate rotation
variants: A surface can only push straight out of itself. On a ramp just part of the weight presses that way, so N = m*g*cos(theta), and the leftover part is what slides the object down the slope.
On flat ground cos(theta) is at its largest and the surface carries the full weight m*g. Tilt the ramp and cos(theta) shrinks, so N = m*g*cos(theta) drops. Stand it upright and it carries nothing.

Turn your axes to line up with the ramp and the weight splits in two. The part pressing into the surface is N = m*g*cos(theta). The rest runs down along the slope, and unless friction holds it, you slide.

name: Work-energy theorem
anchor: net work shows up as motion, so you never track the force step by step
variants: Do net work on something and it speeds up. The work does not vanish, it turns into motion, and W_net = K_B - K_A says how much: the kinetic energy at the end minus the kinetic energy at the start.
Push a crate while friction drags back on it. Add up the work from every force, not just yours, and that total is W_net = K_B - K_A. If friction wins it goes negative and the crate ends up slower.
You never have to follow the force step by step. Take the kinetic energy at B, subtract what it was at A, and that difference is the net work: W_net = K_B - K_A, whatever route it took to get there.

name: Drag force
anchor: cyclist tucking, C measured in a wind tunnel, slow dust falls as v not v^2
variants: Move through air or water and it pushes back, harder the faster you go. Drag is F_D = (1/2)*C*rho*A*v^2, so doubling your speed quadruples the push. That is why a cyclist tucks.
Drag climbs with the square of speed: F_D = (1/2)*C*rho*A*v^2. You can measure A and rho, but C is the penalty for your shape, and it comes out of a wind tunnel, not out of theory.
Air does not just slow you down, it fights harder the faster you shove. F_D = (1/2)*C*rho*A*v^2, always opposing the motion. For dust drifting slowly, though, drag goes as v, not v^2.

name: Period of a particle's motion in a magnetic field
anchor: speed cancels out of the period, which is what lets a cyclotron use one fixed rate
variants: Fling a charge into a magnetic field and it circles. The surprise is in T = (2*pi*m)/(q*B): no speed appears. Go faster and you just carve a wider circle in exactly the same time.
Magnetic force turns a charge without speeding it up, so the path closes into a loop. One lap takes T = (2*pi*m)/(q*B). Cyclotrons live on that: one fixed kick rate fits every lap, slow or fast.
Only m, q and B set the timing here: T = (2*pi*m)/(q*B). Heavier particle, slower lap. Crank up B and the loops tighten and quicken. How hard you threw it in never enters.

name: area of a sector
anchor: pizza slice, radians not degrees, a full turn hands back the whole disc
variants: Picture a pizza slice. Its area is A = (1/2)*theta*r^2, so the same angle off a bigger pizza wins you much more: stretch r and the slice grows with r^2, not with r.
Cut a wedge from a disk and you keep a fraction of it, set by how far the wedge opens. That is A = (1/2)*theta*r^2. One catch: theta has to be in radians. Feed it degrees and you get junk.
Open the wedge wider and the area rises straight with theta; push the rim out and it rises with r^2. Both sit in A = (1/2)*theta*r^2. Let theta swing a full turn and you get the whole disc.

name: output work after friction losses
anchor: warm drill bit, crate up a ramp, the lost work is heat and not destruction
variants: Work does not vanish, it gets skimmed. Put W_in into a machine, friction takes W_f as heat, and you keep W_out = W_in - W_f. Feel a drill bit after a long cut: that is the missing part.
Shove a crate up a ramp and some of your effort never reaches the top. W_out = W_in - W_f. The lost work is not destroyed, it warms the ramp. Every real machine leaks some this way.
W_out = W_in - W_f is bookkeeping. What you put in either does the job or heats the rubbing surfaces, nothing else. Polish the contact and W_out climbs toward W_in, but never past it.

name: resistance from voltage and current
anchor: current shoving past atoms and heating them, a tired battery going flat
variants: Resistance is how stubborn a path is. Push V across it, see how much current I squeezes through, and R = V/I is the score. Same push, less current through, higher resistance.
R = V/I, and nothing exotic is going on: the current has to shove past the atoms of the material, and they heat up taking the hits. Your charger going warm is R doing its work.
Every piece of a circuit has an R = V/I, even the inside of a battery. As a battery wears out its own resistance climbs, so it can no longer push much current, and it reads as flat.

name: normal force on an object on a horizontal surface
anchor: bathroom scale reads the push, not a third-law pair, and it fails on a ramp
variants: The table pushes back. Sit still on a flat surface and your weight pulls down while the surface holds you up just as hard, so N = m*g. Tilt that surface and it stops being true.
N = m*g is not Newton's third law, it comes from the second. You are not accelerating, so the upward push has to cancel the downward pull exactly. Gravity and the floor are not a pair.
Your bathroom scale reads the floor pushing up on you, not gravity pulling down. On level ground those match, so N = m*g. Ride an elevator, or stand on a ramp, and the reading shifts.

name: frequency from wavelength
anchor: a band across a stadium staying in step, one family from radio to visible light
variants: Waves trade length for rate: f = c/lambda. If speed depended on pitch, a band across a stadium would reach you out of step, bass lagging the treble. One speed for all, so short waves arrive more often.
Count the crests going past you each second and that is f. Pack them closer and more arrive: f = c/lambda. Halve lambda and f doubles, because c does not budge to make room.
Radio waves, microwaves, visible light: one family, all running at c, told apart only by lambda. f = c/lambda swaps one label for the other. Long waves count slowly, short ones count fast.

name: total entropy change of system and surroundings
anchor: the second law as bookkeeping, reversible limit of zero, heat not running uphill
variants: Entropy is not conserved, it piles up. Take the change at the hot end, add the change at the cold end: Delta_S_tot = Delta_S_h + Delta_S_c. For anything that really happens the total is positive.

Push heat from hot to cold and the cold side gains more entropy than the hot side loses, because it is colder. So Delta_S_tot = Delta_S_h + Delta_S_c leans positive, and that lean is the second law itself.
Delta_S_tot = Delta_S_h + Delta_S_c watches both ends of a heat flow at once. Only a reversible step holds it at zero; a real temperature gap always pushes it up. Heat will not run back uphill.

name: Angular acceleration
variants: Spin a bike wheel up by hand and it takes a few seconds; grab the brake and it stops fast. Angular acceleration is that difference: alpha = (Delta_omega)/(Delta_t), how quickly the spin rate changes.
A skater pulls her arms in and speeds up. How fast a spin rate changes is alpha = (Delta_omega)/(Delta_t). Same idea as everyday acceleration, just for turning. Braking makes alpha oppose the spin.

Angular acceleration asks how fast a spin is changing, not how fast it spins. alpha = (Delta_omega)/(Delta_t). A disk coasting down has a small alpha; a wheel caught by a brake has a big one, the other way.

name: angular acceleration from tangential acceleration
variants: Every point on a spinning disk shares one alpha, but a point out on the rim gains speed faster than one near the axle. Divide out how far out you are and you get the shared number back: alpha = (a_t)/(r).

Stand at the edge of a merry-go-round as it starts and you get shoved harder than someone near the middle. Their a_t differs, alpha does not. alpha = (a_t)/(r) recovers the one alpha the whole ride shares.

Speeding up along the circle and speeding up the spin are one event described two ways. They differ only by how far out you measure it, so alpha = (a_t)/(r). The radius has to stay fixed for that to hold.

name: net force from rate of momentum change
variants: A force is really a delivery rate for momentum. F_net = (Delta_p)/(Delta_t), so the same momentum change spread over a longer time takes less force. That is what an airbag and a bent knee are buying you.
A racquet turns a tennis ball around in a few thousandths of a second, so the force is enormous. F_net = (Delta_p)/(Delta_t) says force is momentum change per time. Short contact, big force.

Newton wrote his second law this way first. F_net = (Delta_p)/(Delta_t). Hold mass steady and it becomes force equals mass times acceleration, but this version survives when mass is leaving, as in a rocket.

name: definition of electric potential
variants: Voltage is energy per unit charge, not energy. V = (U_E)/(q) divides out how much charge you brought, so what is left describes the spot itself, and any charge dropped there gets that much per coulomb.
Two charges at one spot hold different energies if one carries more charge. Divide by the charge and that difference goes away: V = (U_E)/(q). It is why a battery is rated in volts and not in joules.
Think of potential as what the field charges per coulomb. V = (U_E)/(q), so U_E depends on what you carry and V does not. Bring a charge q to that spot and the energy it holds is q times V.

name: resultant velocity from component velocities
variants: Velocities along the same line just add. Your own v_p plus the air or water moving with you, v_wy, gives v_toty = v_wy + v_p. A tailwind gets you home early; a headwind is the same sum with v_wy negative.

Swim downstream and the current is free speed. Along one axis your speed over the ground is v_toty = v_wy + v_p, the push you ride plus your own. Turn upstream and v_p goes negative, so the sum shrinks.

You add velocities one axis at a time. Point a plane due north and all of its own speed lands there: v_toty = v_wy + v_p. The sideways wind gets its own separate sum, and that is what drifts it off course.

name: acceleration from force and mass
variants: Push a basketball and push an SUV with the same force and only one of them goes anywhere. a = (F)/(m) says acceleration climbs with force and falls with mass. Mass is just how stubborn a thing is.

Newton's second law, solved for the part you usually want. a = (F)/(m). Double the push and the acceleration doubles; double the mass and it halves. F is the net force, everything pushing and dragging added up.
Motion does not need force; changing motion does. a = (F)/(m), and a points wherever F points. Push a mower along at steady speed and friction is cancelling you, so F is zero and so is a.

name: Energy change associated with ionic bonding
variants: Making table salt costs energy to hand an electron from sodium to chlorine, E_transfer, and pays it back when the two ions pull together, U_coul. Add the close-in push-back U_ex: U_form = E_transfer + U_coul + U_ex.

An ionic bond is a three-line ledger. U_form = E_transfer + U_coul + U_ex: the price of moving the electron, the payoff from opposite charges attracting, and the shove back when the ions crowd too close.

Why does sodium stick to chlorine at all? U_form = E_transfer + U_coul + U_ex. The Coulomb term is the payoff, U_ex keeps the ions from collapsing together, and a negative total means the bond is worth making.

name: position under constant acceleration
variants: Where you end up is where you started, plus where steady speed carries you, plus whatever the acceleration adds: d = d_0+v_0*t+(1/2)*a*t^2. Both d and d_0 are measured from the same origin.
Throw a rock off a cliff and this tracks it the whole way down: d = d_0+v_0*t+(1/2)*a*t^2. The squared term is why falling gets dramatic late. It holds only while a stays constant.
Three pieces, and the last one is the one to watch. In d = d_0+v_0*t+(1/2)*a*t^2 that term grows with time squared: nothing early, everything later. And d is a position, not a distance covered.
