name: rms current from impedance
anchor: no evidence and no glossary; rms as the DC-equivalent heating value
variants: The rms numbers are the ones that act like DC: an rms amp heats a resistor exactly as a steady amp would. That is why I_rms = V_rms/Z is written in them, with Z the circuit's total opposition.

Swap resistance for impedance and Ohm's law still works on alternating current: I_rms = V_rms/Z. Unlike a resistor, Z depends on how fast the current alternates, so the same voltage drives a different current.
A coil fights a current that is changing, and a capacitor blocks one that is steady. Roll all of that opposition into a single number Z and the old rule comes straight back: I_rms = V_rms/Z.

name: impulse-momentum theorem
anchor: OpenStax: bend your knees when jumping, car crumple zones, racket hitting a ball
variants: Bend your knees when you land and you stretch the stop over more time. Same change in momentum, much smaller force, because Delta_p = F_net*Delta_t. A force only counts for as long as it acts.
A racquet hits a ball hard for an instant. A gentle shove does the same job if you keep pushing. Both give the same Delta_p = F_net*Delta_t, so what changes motion is force multiplied by time.
Newton wrote his second law this way first: Delta_p = F_net*Delta_t. It is why cars are built to crumple. The stop takes longer, so the force on you drops while your momentum change is fixed.

name: equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel
anchor: OpenStax: reduce the pair to one resistor so Ohm's law gives the circuit current
variants: Give the current two paths and more of it gets through, so the pair resists less than either one alone. R_eqv = 1/(1/R_1 + 1/R_2). Collapse them to that number and Ohm's law handles the rest.
Add a resistor in parallel and the resistance goes down, not up, because you have opened another lane. R_eqv = 1/(1/R_1 + 1/R_2), and it always lands below the smaller of R_1 and R_2.
The trick is that conductances add, not resistances. Flip each one, add them, flip back: R_eqv = 1/(1/R_1 + 1/R_2). Now the branch is a single resistor and you can get the current through it.

name: The de Broglie wavelength
anchor: OpenStax: de Broglie's thesis and Einstein's backing; electron diffraction off crystals
variants: A graduate student guessed that nature is symmetric: if light can act like a particle, matter should act like a wave. Einstein read the thesis and backed him. The guess was lambda = h/p, and it held up.

Every moving thing has a wavelength, lambda = h/p. You never notice yours because h is tiny and your momentum is not, so the wavelength comes out far too small to measure. Shrink p to an electron and it shows.
Fire electrons at a crystal and they land in a diffraction pattern, which is what waves do. The wavelength that fits is lambda = h/p, h being Planck's constant and p the momentum. Matter is wavy too.

name: total mechanical energy
anchor: OpenStax: roller coaster trading height for speed, and the closed-system friction caveat
variants: On a roller coaster the car trades height for speed the whole way round. E = K + U is the running total, K for the motion and U for the height. With no friction that total never changes.
Energy a thing has from moving, plus energy it has from where it sits: E = K + U. The sum is what makes it useful, because in a closed system K and U keep swapping while E stays put.
E = K + U only holds a fixed value while nothing rubs. Friction and air drag leak energy off as heat and the mechanical total drops. The closed-system wording is a real condition, not a formality.

name: Centripetal force
anchor: OpenStax list: rope tension, road friction, gravity on the Moon; glossary's perpendicular component
variants: Centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is the name for whatever is already pulling you inward: rope tension, road friction, Earth's pull on the Moon. Whatever does the job, F_c = m*a_c.
Rounding a bend is accelerating even at steady speed, because your direction keeps changing. Something has to supply that, and F_c = m*a_c says how much. For a car it is friction on the tires.
The part of the net force pointing sideways to your motion turns you instead of speeding you up. That part is F_c = m*a_c. Take it away, as on ice, and you stop turning and carry straight on.

name: Fermi temperature
anchor: no evidence paragraphs; one-line glossary only, so written from the physics
variants: Divide the Fermi energy by Boltzmann's constant and an energy becomes a temperature: T_F = E_F/k_B. It is how hot you would have to get an ordinary particle to make it move as fast as those electrons do.
Warm a metal wire and the electrons inside barely notice. The Fermi energy written as a temperature, T_F = E_F/k_B, sits far above anything you could heat the wire to, so heating hardly stirs them.
Electrons in a metal cannot all sit still, so the top ones carry the Fermi energy E_F even at absolute zero. Ask what temperature would give a normal particle that much, and you get T_F = E_F/k_B.

name: Kirchhoff junction rule
anchor: OpenStax: water-pipe junction analogy; a junction is three or more wires; one equation per junction
variants: Charge does not pile up at a wire joint, any more than water piles up in a pipe tee. What flows in flows out: I_1 = I_2 + I_3. That is conservation of charge, written for one junction.
A junction is where three or more wires meet, and the current has to split there. I_1 = I_2 + I_3 says the branches carry off everything the one wire brought in. The joint stores nothing.
Each junction hands you one equation, which is what makes the rule worth having: I_1 = I_2 + I_3. Collect enough of them and you can solve for currents you cannot reach with a meter.

name: input work
anchor: OpenStax lever example: effort arm travels far under a small force; friction wastes the rest as heat
variants: Shove a crate up a ramp and the work you put in is your push times how far you pushed: W_i = F_i*d_i. Push half as hard and you walk twice as far. A machine trades force for distance, never for free.
Feed a machine energy and this is the bill: effort force times the distance you move it, W_i = F_i*d_i. You never get all of it back out. Friction skims some off as heat in every moving joint.
On a lever you press the long arm down a long way with a gentle force. That product is the input work, W_i = F_i*d_i, and the load rises a short way instead. That swap is why it feels easy.

name: heat from internal energy change and work
anchor: OpenStax first law: heat and work are both energy in transit, neither stored as such
variants: Heat poured into something has two places to go: it can raise the energy stored inside, or the thing can push on the world. Q = Delta_E_int + W is the whole ledger. Energy has nowhere else to hide.

Trap a gas in a cylinder and warm it, and two things happen at once. It gets hotter inside and it shoves the piston out. Q = Delta_E_int + W splits the heat between them, and that split is engine design.
You cannot tell, from a warm object, whether it was heated or worked on. Both are energy in transit. Q = Delta_E_int + W splits heat going in between the part that stays and the work that leaves.

name: energy from power and time
anchor: OpenStax energy consumption: the meter charges for the product, billed in kilowatt hours
variants: Power is the rate, energy is the total. Leave something running twice as long and it uses twice as much: E = P*t. A kilowatt hour on your bill is nothing but that product, priced.
A bright lamp for a moment can cost you the same as a dim one left on all night. E = P*t is why. The meter only ever sees the product, so watts alone never tell you what you owe.
Halve the power and run it twice as long and the same energy arrives, because E = P*t and only the product counts. A trickle charger fills the same battery as a fast one; it just takes all night.

name: angular speed
anchor: OpenStax spinning CD: every point shares one omega, and a radian is a ratio of two lengths
variants: Angular speed asks one thing: how fast is the angle changing. Sweep an angle theta in time t and omega = theta/t. Every point on a spinning disk shares that omega, even the rim that travels furthest.
Forget distance and count turning instead. omega = theta/t is the rate the angle grows, in radians per second. A radian is a ratio of two lengths, so theta carries no units of its own.
A clock's second hand holds a perfectly steady omega = theta/t: the same angle, every second, forever. Angular speed is about turning, and it says nothing at all about how long the hand is.

name: extension from length change
anchor: no evidence supplied; extension as displacement away from natural length
variants: A spring does not care how long it is, only how much longer than it likes to be. x = l - l_0 is that difference: length now, minus its natural resting length. Squash it instead and x goes negative.
Measure the bar now, subtract what it measured before you pulled, and the stretch itself is what is left: x = l - l_0. Spring laws want x, not l, because a rest length is not a deformation.
Hang a mass on a spring and the pointer drops. That drop is x = l - l_0, the new length minus the old one. When x is zero the spring sits at its natural length and pushes back on nothing at all.

name: Transformer equation with current
anchor: supplied paragraph is mutual inductance, not the current ratio; written from ideal-transformer power conservation and a welder's thick secondary
variants: Wind more turns on one side and you trade current away for voltage. I_S = (N_P/N_S)*I_P, so the coil with fewer turns carries the bigger current. A transformer reshapes power, it cannot make it.
The fat cable on a welder gives the game away. Few turns on that side, so I_S = (N_P/N_S)*I_P makes its current enormous while the voltage across it falls to almost nothing.
Voltage and current move opposite ways across a transformer. I_S = (N_P/N_S)*I_P flips the turns ratio upside down, because whatever power goes into the primary has to come back out the secondary.

name: fringe spacing in double-slit interference
anchor: no evidence supplied; Young's double-slit geometry
variants: Shine a laser through two close slits and the wall lights up in evenly spaced bands. Delta_y = x*lambda/d is the gap between them. Squeeze the slits closer and the pattern spreads wider apart.
Red bands sit further apart than blue ones, and that is all Delta_y = x*lambda/d is saying. Longer lambda, wider spacing. Back the screen away and they spread too, which is why x sits on top.
Young split one beam in two and let the halves overlap again. Where crest meets crest you get a bright band, spaced by Delta_y = x*lambda/d. Light that does this is light behaving like a wave.

name: photon energy from wavelength
anchor: OpenStax quantization: one visible photon is a tiny fraction of a joule, and Planck was reluctant to accept his own idea
variants: Shorter wavelength, fatter lump of energy. That is all E = (h*c)/lambda says. Blue photons hit harder than red ones, which is why ultraviolet burns your skin and radio waves never will.
Squeeze the wavelength and the energy in one photon climbs: E = (h*c)/lambda. A single photon of visible light is a tiny sliver of a joule, which is why you never notice them landing one by one.

Planck explained glowing hot objects only by assuming energy comes in packets, and he disliked his own idea. Einstein carried it to light itself. E = (h*c)/lambda sizes one packet: color alone sets it.

name: density from mass and volume
variants: Pack more mass into the same box and it gets denser. That is all rho = m/V is. Archimedes was handed the job of checking whether a king's crown was really gold, and this is the number that answers it.
Weigh an old coin, measure the water it pushes aside, divide: rho = m/V. Pure silver gives one number and a fake gives another. Density does not care how big the piece is, only what it is made of.
A solid steel block sinks. Beat the same steel into a hull and it floats, because the V in rho = m/V is now the whole boat, air included. Same mass, far more volume, so the average density drops.

name: Common expression of Ohm's law
variants: Voltage is the push, current is the flow, resistance is how much the wire fights back. V = I*R ties the three together: same push against more resistance, and less current gets through.
Double the voltage across a resistor and you double the current. That is all Ohm's law says, V = I*R. It is not a law of nature though. Plenty of parts, a diode for one, ignore it completely.
Think of water in a pipe. V = I*R says the pressure you need is the flow you want times how narrow the pipe is. Narrow it, and pushing the same current through suddenly costs a lot more voltage.

name: photon energy from frequency
variants: Light does not arrive in a smooth stream. It comes in packets, and E = h*f says a packet's energy is set by its frequency alone. Planck guessed it for hot glowing objects; Einstein saw what it meant.

Violet light hits harder per photon than red does, because E = h*f and violet has the higher frequency. Turning the lamp up sends more photons, not stronger ones. One is enough to fire a cell in your eye.
A molecule only swallows a photon whose energy matches a step it can climb, and E = h*f fixes that energy by frequency. Violet flowers soak up the red and throw the violet back. So they look violet.

name: power
variants: Power is not how much work you do, it is how fast. P = W/t. Carry the boxes upstairs in one trip or in ten and the work is the same, but do it in half the time and you needed twice the power.
A watt is one joule every second, and that is all P = W/t says: the work divided by the time it took. A light bulb quietly spends joules the whole time it is on, and that steady rate is its power.
Same job, less time, more power, and P = W/t is the bookkeeping. It is why a car that accelerates hard drinks fuel. It does a lot of work in a few seconds, and the engine has to deliver it that fast.

name: average speed
variants: Drive to the store and back and your average velocity is zero, but your average speed is not. v = d/t uses the ground your odometer counted, not where you ended up. Speed carries no direction.

Your speedometer tells you about right now. v = d/t tells you about the whole trip: total distance over total time, every red light included. It is an average, so it hides the speeding up and slowing down.

A winding road covers more ground than the map shows. The d in v = d/t is the path you actually drove, every curve of it, not the straight line between the ends. Speed counts detours; velocity does not.

name: Newton's second law
variants: Push two things with the same force and the heavier one barely budges. F = m*a says it straight: acceleration is what the force buys you, and mass is the price. Mass is a measure of that stubbornness.
F = m*a is a trade. A given force, divided by however much mass you are shoving. It assumes the mass holds steady, so it quietly fails on a rocket, which is busy burning away a good part of itself.

Nothing speeds up on its own. Something has to push, and F = m*a says how much you get for the push. Drop a rock and gravity is the only push worth counting, so it keeps gaining speed the whole way down.
anchor: mass as a measure of inertia; the rocket that breaks the law by burning away its own mass

name: kinetic energy
variants: Double your speed and you carry four times the energy, not twice. That squared v in K = 0.5*m*v^2 is the whole story. Mass counts too, but speed is the one that punishes you for it.

K = 0.5*m*v^2 is the energy a thing has purely because it is moving. It is not the last word. Get a particle near the speed of light and the true answer runs away from this one. At normal speeds they agree.

A helicopter flying along has kinetic energy, and so do the blades whirling overhead, but K = 0.5*m*v^2 only covers the first. Every point on a blade moves at its own speed, so blades need their own version.
anchor: the squared v; the relativistic and rotational limits where the formula stops holding

name: gravitational potential energy
variants: Lifting something is a loan. U = m*g*h is what you handed over, and gravity collects it on the way down. Let go and it comes back as speed. Hang it in a cuckoo clock and it comes back as ticking.

There is no true height. In U = m*g*h you pick where h starts from, so a hiker down at sea level ends up with a negative number if you measured from the trailhead. Only the change between two spots is real.
Twice the mass, or twice the height, twice the stored energy: U = m*g*h. The g is in there because nothing gets stored unless something is pulling back down on you the whole way up.
anchor: the arbitrary zero for h (the hiker at sea level goes negative); the cuckoo clock weight

name: momentum
anchor: Newton called it quantity of motion in the Principia; racket hitting a tennis ball
variants: Momentum is how hard a thing is to stop. p = m*v, so a slow truck can carry more of it than a sprinting person. Newton wrote his second law this way first and called it the quantity of motion.
Two things make you hard to stop: being heavy and being fast. p = m*v folds both into one number. It has a direction too, and in a crash the total before and after comes out the same.
A racquet touches a ball for a blink and sends it flying. What it changed was p = m*v. To change it you need a force, and the longer that force acts, the more of it you change.

name: work done by a constant force
anchor: carrying a briefcase horizontally does zero work; the lawn mower pushed at an angle
variants: Carry a heavy bag across a room and you do no work on it. Work is W = F*d, force times the distance moved along that force. You pull up, the bag goes sideways, so none of it counts.
Push a mower and only the part of your push that points where it rolls does anything. That is W = F*d. Shove at an angle and some of the effort never turns into work at all.
W = F*d is the energy a force hands over. Push something along and you give it energy. Push against the motion, the way gravity does on a ball going up, and the work comes out negative.

name: centripetal acceleration
anchor: centripetal is Latin for center seeking; the square means twice the speed is four times the acceleration
variants: Round a curve at steady speed and you are still accelerating, because your direction keeps changing. a = v^2/r points straight at the center. Centripetal is Latin for center seeking.
Take a bend twice as fast and the car has to haul you inward four times as hard. That is the square in a = v^2/r. Speed dominates, and a tight curve, meaning a small r, makes it worse again.
Nothing pulls you outward in a turn. a = v^2/r is the acceleration aimed inward that keeps you on the circle, and what you feel is the seat shoving you toward the center to supply it.

name: electrical power
anchor: electricity bills are sold in kilowatt-hours, power multiplied by time
variants: Voltage is energy per charge, current is charge per second. Multiply and the charge cancels, leaving energy per second, which is power: P = V*I. Same watts from a big V or a big I.
Your electric bill is P = V*I stretched over hours. That is what a kilowatt hour is. Double the current at the same voltage and the appliance eats energy twice as fast.
P = V*I is the rate a device drains energy, not the amount it holds. A kettle pulls a heavy current from the wall and boils fast. A phone charger sips at the same voltage.

name: torque
anchor: push the merry-go-round as far from the center as possible for the largest lever arm
variants: Push a merry-go-round near the middle and little happens. Push at the rim and it spins. Same force, bigger r. tau = r*F is twisting effort, and distance from the pivot counts as much as push.
A long wrench beats a short one on the same bolt, because tau = r*F grows with r. You cannot always push harder, but you can push farther out. That is the whole idea behind handles.
Torque is force plus leverage: tau = r*F. Push straight in at the pivot and nothing turns however hard you shove. The push has to cut across the arm, and a longer arm wins.

name: drift velocity in crossed electric and magnetic fields
anchor: no evidence and no glossary in the file; written from the velocity selector, where the electric and magnetic forces balance at one speed
variants: Cross an electric field with a magnetic one and a charge gets two opposite shoves. They cancel at exactly one speed, v_d = E/B. Go faster or slower and you get bent out of the beam.
v_d = E/B is a speed filter. The charge cancels out of it, so every particle obeys the same number whatever it is. Mass spectrometers use this to pick one speed before sorting by mass.
A charge sitting still here feels only the electric push. Start it moving and the magnetic force fights back, growing with speed, until at v_d = E/B the two balance and it sails straight.

name: pressure at depth in a fluid
anchor: pressure depends only on depth and not on the shape of the container; constant density fails in the atmosphere
variants: Your ears hurt at the deep end because a column of water is sitting on you. p = p_0 + rho*g*h adds that weight to the air already pressing down. Only the depth h matters, not the pool shape.
Pressure under water is what the air pushes plus what the water above adds: p = p_0 + rho*g*h. Swim sideways and nothing changes. Go down and it climbs steadily the whole way.
Sink twice as deep and the water share of the pressure doubles. p = p_0 + rho*g*h works because water barely squashes, so rho holds still. Air does squash, so the sky needs other math.

name: magnetic force on a moving charge
anchor: this relation is what defines the tesla, named after Nikola Tesla; zero force when moving along the field
variants: Park a charge in a magnetic field and nothing happens to it. Give it a speed across the field and it feels F = q*v*B. That is why a magnet ignores a still charge but grabs a wire carrying current.
The magnetic force pushes sideways to the motion, so F = q*v*B steers a charge rather than speeding it up. Paths bend into circles. That is how an accelerator holds a beam on its ring.

F = q*v*B is the full force only when the charge cuts straight across the field. Fly along the field lines instead and you feel nothing. This relation is what defines the tesla, named for Nikola Tesla.

name: electric potential of a point charge
anchor: OpenStax Electric Potential: pressure-in-a-pipe analogy, scalar superposition
variants: Think of it as pressure in a pipe: a loose positive charge slides from high potential toward low. Near a point charge q that pressure is V = k_e*q/r, falling off steadily as you back away.
It is the energy per coulomb needed to haul a test charge in from far away and park it a distance r from q. V = k_e*q/r. Per unit charge, so it does not care what you bring to probe it.
Potentials add as plain numbers, with no arrows to chase. Each nearby charge kicks in its own V = k_e*q/r and you total them, which is why voltage is friendlier to work with than the field.

name: electric field at a charged conducting surface
anchor: OpenStax: field at one plate depends only on that plate's sigma; air sparks
variants: Pack charge onto a conductor and the field just outside its skin depends only on how densely the charge sits there: E = sigma/epsilon_0. No distance in it, no size of the object either.
Here is the odd part. Face two oppositely charged plates and the field at one surface still cares only about that plate's own charge density, E = sigma/epsilon_0. The other plate does not enter.
Crowd charge onto a surface and E = sigma/epsilon_0 climbs until the air itself quits insulating and sparks. sigma is charge per square meter; epsilon_0 sets how stiffly empty space pushes back.

name: Newton's law of universal gravitation
anchor: OpenStax: apple and Moon obey one rule, Cavendish measured G a century later
variants: You and this calculator are pulling on each other right now. F = G*m1*m2/r^2 says every pair of masses does, and the pull dies fast: back off to twice the distance, get a quarter the force.
Newton's leap was that the falling apple and the orbiting Moon obey one rule, with the same G everywhere in the universe. F = G*m1*m2/r^2. Cavendish only measured G a century later.
Your weight is this force with Earth as one of the masses. F = G*m1*m2/r^2, so haul yourself to the Moon and the pull shrinks even though the matter in you has not changed one bit.

name: heat transferred with no phase change
anchor: OpenStax Phase Change: temperature stays flat while melting, so it quits there
variants: Heat something and the energy it soaks up is Q = m*c*dT: more mass or a bigger temperature swing costs more joules. It quits at the melting point, where heat pours in and dT stays flat.
c is how stubborn the substance is. Water demands a lot of energy per degree, most metals almost none. Q = m*c*dT scales that by how much you have and how far you moved the temperature.
Why beach sand scorches your feet while the sea stays cold: same sun, but Q = m*c*dT and water's c is huge, so the same heat buys the water a far smaller dT than it buys the sand.

name: uniform acceleration
anchor: OpenStax Constant Acceleration: falling objects; non-constant force breaks it
variants: Acceleration is how fast your speed is changing. a = (vf-vi)/t: the speed you ended with, minus the one you started with, over the time it took. Slow down instead and a comes out negative.
Drop something and it gains the same chunk of speed every second. That sameness is what uniform means, and a = (vf-vi)/t only tells the truth while it holds. A car in traffic breaks it constantly.
The shove that pins you into a car seat is this. a = (vf-vi)/t spreads the whole change in velocity evenly across t, so it is the real acceleration only if the rate never wavered in between.

name: displacement under uniform acceleration
anchor: no evidence paragraphs; written from the two-term structure of the formula
variants: Two trips added together: how far you would coast a*t vi, plus the extra the acceleration piles on. d = vi*t+0.5*a*t^2. That second piece grows with t squared, so it takes over quickly.
Start from rest and the vi*t term vanishes, leaving only the 0.5*a*(t)^(2) half. Double the time and you cover four times the ground, which is why a dropped ball seems to cheat near the end.
It tells you where you ended up, not how far you drove. Brake hard from vi and a turns negative in d = vi*t+0.5*a*t^2, so the second term eats into the first instead of adding to it.

name: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor
anchor: OpenStax Parallel Plate Capacitor: bigger A spreads charge, farad is huge
variants: Capacitance is how much charge two plates hold per volt. Wide plates give charge room to spread out, close plates tug harder on each other, so C = epsilon_0*(A/d). Nothing else gets a say.
A farad is a monstrous unit. epsilon_0 is tiny and C = epsilon_0*(A/d), so plates the size of a desk barely register, which is why real capacitors are long thin foils rolled up tight.
Pull the plates apart and the capacitance drops, because d sits underneath in C = epsilon_0*(A/d). Only geometry appears, so it is settled long before any battery ever gets wired up.

name: Distance
anchor: OpenStax Distance: professor paces a long path, ends near her start; no sign
variants: It is Pythagoras wearing a coat. Go x_2-x_1 across and y_2-y_1 up, and the straight line closing that right triangle is d = sqrt((x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2). Works on any flat map.
A teacher pacing the front of a room all lecture walks a long way and still finishes a stride from where she began. d = sqrt((x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2) measures that gap, not the path.
Swap the two points and nothing changes: squaring wipes out the minus signs, so d = sqrt((x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2) has no direction and never comes out negative. The two legs combine, they do not add.

name: Wave speed
anchor: guitar string: the medium bobs, the pattern travels
variants: Watch a wave cross a rope. The rope never travels, the shape does, and v = omega/k is how fast that shape moves. omega is the cycling in time, k the cycling in space, and speed is the ratio.
How hard you pluck changes nothing about how fast a wave crosses. Its speed is the cycling in time, omega, over how tightly it repeats in space, k: v = omega/k. The string decides that, not you.
The bit of string in front of you only bobs up and down; the pattern is what moves, at v = omega/k. Thick heavy strings carry it slower, which is why they sound lower than thin ones.

name: energy difference from a frequency difference
anchor: Planck disbelieving his own h; the K/L shell X-ray gap
variants: Energy in light comes in lumps, not a smooth stream. Step up in frequency by Delta_f and the energy step is Delta_E = h*Delta_f. Planck got h from glowing hot objects and did not believe it himself.

The steps are so small that energy looks perfectly smooth to you, because h is a tiny number. Delta_E = h*Delta_f turns a gap in frequency into a gap in energy. Widen the jump, the photon carries more.
Two shells in an atom sit some energy apart, and the photon bridging them carries exactly that gap. Delta_E = h*Delta_f. Deep shells are far apart, so what they emit comes out as X-rays.

name: Drift velocity
anchor: the light comes on instantly while electrons crawl
variants: Flip a switch and the light comes on at once, but the electrons themselves barely crawl. v_d = I/(n*q*A) is that crawl. More carriers n or a fatter wire A, and each charge can go slower for the same I.

A*n electron in a wire ricochets around fast and nearly at random. Underneath the chaos is a slow average drift, v_d = I/(n*q*A). Copper packs in so many free charges that the drift is slower than a snail.

Current is charge per second. Take the charge sitting in each cubic meter, n*q, times the wire's area A, then divide the current by it: v_d = I/(n*q*A). A*n average over a crowd, not one electron's dash.

name: wavelength from frequency
anchor: measuring c with a microwave and a slice of bread
variants: Speed is set by the medium, so frequency and wavelength trade off: lambda = c/f. Raise f and the crests bunch up. It is why an AM aerial is the size of a tower and a wifi one fits in a laptop.
You can check this with a microwave and a slice of bread. The scorched spots sit half a wavelength apart, the frequency is printed on the back, and lambda = c/f gives you the speed in your kitchen.
A band in a stadium stays in cadence however far off you stand, because in one medium every pitch shares a speed. Call it c and lambda = c/f follows: the higher the note, the shorter its wave.

name: Definition of weight, scalar form
anchor: no evidence and no glossary in the record; written from physics
variants: Mass is how much of you there is. Weight is how hard a planet pulls on that. w = m*g, so fly to the Moon and m does not budge, but g drops, and the reading on the scale drops with it.
Your bathroom scale never measures you. It measures the push it takes to hold you up, w = m*g. Change g and the number changes. That is why weight is in newtons while mass stays in kilograms.
A feather and an anvil feel the same g, so w = m*g rides entirely on mass. The heavy one is pulled harder but has more mass to move, so with the air taken away they fall side by side.

name: period
anchor: the OpenStax paycheck analogy, twice a month
variants: Period and frequency are one fact said two ways, T = 1/f. Paid twice a month? That is the frequency. The half month of waiting between checks is the period. Count the events, or count the wait.
Count how many swings land in a second and you have f. Ask instead how long a single swing takes and you have T = 1/f. Quick repeats mean a short wait, and there is nothing more to it than that.
Hang a mass on a spring and each bounce takes the same time whether you pull it far or barely at all. That time is T, and T = 1/f: counts per second one way, seconds per count the other.

name: angular speed from angular displacement
anchor: flywheel energy storage on near frictionless bearings
variants: Angular speed is plain speed with angle swapped in for distance: omega = Delta_theta/Delta_t. A spinning wheel has one omega everywhere, and the rim still outruns the hub, having farther to go.

A clock's second hand sweeps the same slice of the circle every second, so its omega = Delta_theta/Delta_t holds steady. Angle is a bare number with no unit of its own, so omega is a plain per second.
A flywheel banks energy by holding a big omega = Delta_theta/Delta_t. Set it on near frictionless bearings and it keeps sweeping the same angle every second for a very long time.

name: Height of free fall
anchor: Galileo: feather and anvil fall together without air
variants: Begin where it left your hand, add how far the throw alone would carry it, then subtract what gravity claws back: y = y_0 + v_0*t - (1/2)*g*t^2. The minus sign is why g goes in as a size, not a direction.
Gravity pulls just as hard per kilogram on a feather as on an anvil, so mass never shows up here: y = y_0 + v_0*t - (1/2)*g*t^2. Galileo was right. Let air drag matter and it stops holding.
The throw part grows steadily, the gravity part grows faster and faster, and when the two match, the ball is back at the height it left. y = y_0 + v_0*t - (1/2)*g*t^2 covers the whole arc.

name: magnetic field due to a long straight wire
variants: Push current down a wire and the space around it starts shoving on magnets. The field wraps the wire in circles, B = ((mu_0*I)/(2*pi*R)). Right thumb along the current, fingers curl the way B points.
Stand twice as far from the wire and the field is half as strong. B = ((mu_0*I)/(2*pi*R)), and that 2*pi*R underneath is the circle you are standing on: one current spread round a longer path.
Good only close to a wire that is long compared with R, and mu_0 is just a constant of empty space. B = ((mu_0*I)/(2*pi*R)). Bend the wire and you must add up every little piece instead.
anchor: right-hand rule; field circles the wire; bent wire needs summing segments

name: binding energy of an electron
variants: Shine dim blue light on sodium and electrons jump off. Shine bright red light and nothing comes out at all. There is a threshold frequency f_O, and E_b = h*f_O is how tightly that electron was held.
Photons arrive whole, one photon to one electron, so turning the lamp up only sends more of them. The lowest frequency that frees anything, f_O, measures the grip: E_b = h*f_O.
E_b = h*f_O is the bill for prying one electron off a surface. Light right at f_O pays it exactly, so the electron crawls out with no speed to spare. Redder light never pays, however long you wait.
anchor: photoelectric threshold: bright red light frees nothing, dim blue does

name: Velocity of a wave
variants: A wave travels one whole wavelength in one cycle, so v = f*lambda is really just how far over how long. Count f crests going past you each second, and they arrive lambda apart.
Watch a gull ride the swell: it bobs in place while the wave rolls on past it. v = f*lambda is the speed of the shape, not of the water. The water itself goes nowhere.
The stuff it travels through fixes v, so f and lambda have to trade off: v = f*lambda. That is why a band's low notes and high notes reach the back of the room together.
anchor: the gull bobbing in place while the swell passes under it

name: vertical position from average vertical velocity
variants: Speed up steadily and your average is just the halfway point between the start and the end. That is all this is: y = y_0+(1/2)(v_0y+v_y)t, halfway speed times t, on top of where you began.
Nothing about how hard it speeds up appears here, which is the point. Know the speed at both ends and y = y_0+(1/2)(v_0y+v_y)t hands you the height, with no rate to work out first.
Halving the sum of the two end speeds is an honest average only while the speed changes at a steady rate. Add air drag and y = y_0+(1/2)(v_0y+v_y)t quietly stops being true.
anchor: the midpoint of the two end speeds IS the average, but only under steady gain

name: quantum energy
variants: Energy here comes in whole steps, never slices. E = n*h*f says a wave of frequency f can carry one lump h*f, or two, or n of them, and nothing at all in between.
n is a count, so it runs in whole numbers only: E = n*h*f. A blue flame is more dangerous than a red one because each of its steps is bigger, not because it takes more of them.
Planck put the n in to rescue a broken account of glowing hot metal, and it worked. E = n*h*f. The step h*f is so tiny that we see a ramp; only something atom sized feels the stairs.
anchor: a blue flame is more dangerous than a red one, bigger step not more steps

name: equivalent resistance of two resistors in series
variants: In series there is one path only, so the same current goes through both and their voltage drops add. Hence R_eqv = R_1+R_2. Add more bulbs to a series string and every one of them dims.
Picture one long wire made of two poor stretches joined end to end: R_eqv = R_1+R_2. Wire that same pair side by side instead and you get less resistance than either one alone.
True only while nothing branches off between them. Same current through both, so R_eqv = R_1+R_2. Untangling a messy circuit is mostly spotting such pairs and collapsing them one at a time.
anchor: one path, so the voltage drops add; collapsing a messy circuit pair by pair

name: Centripetal acceleration
variants: Your speed can hold perfectly steady round a bend and you are still being pulled, because your direction keeps changing. a_c = ((v^2)/r), aimed at the center of the turn, never along it.
The v is squared, which catches people out. Take the same curve at twice the speed and the pull on you is four times harder, not twice as hard: a_c = ((v^2)/r).
The outward shove you feel in a turning car is just your body trying to keep going straight. The real pull is inward, a_c = ((v^2)/r), and tightening r makes it bite harder.
anchor: same curve at twice the speed pulls four times harder; the outward shove is fictitious

name: Time of flight
variants: Only the upward part of the launch matters. v_0*sin(theta_0) is the kick straight up, and gravity takes it away then hands it back, so T_tof = ((2(v_0*sin(theta_0)))/g): rise equals fall.
Launch and land at the same height and this is exact: T_tof = ((2(v_0*sin(theta_0)))/g). Let it come down on a roof or in the stands and it breaks, since the fall no longer mirrors the rise.
g sits on the bottom, so the same throw on the Moon hangs far longer. T_tof = ((2(v_0*sin(theta_0)))/g). Aim flatter and sin(theta_0) shrinks with it: a line drive is down long before a pop fly.
anchor: the tennis ball landing up in the stands, where the flat-surface assumption breaks

name: Period of a mass-spring system in SHM
variants: Pluck a guitar string gently or hard and you get the same note. A mass bouncing on a spring is just as stubborn: T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k) has no amplitude in it. More m, slower. Stiffer k, faster.
A heavy person on a diving board bounces up and down more slowly than a light one. That is T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k). Mass sits on top and stretches the period, stiffness k sits underneath and shortens it.

Time one wobble of a mass on a spring: T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k). Look at what is missing. How far you pulled it. Pull it twice as far and it still takes the same time. Overstretching the spring breaks that.
anchor: guitar string plucked gently or hard, and the heavy vs light diver on a diving board, both taken from the OpenStax SHM section

name: mass from energy equivalence
variants: Energy can be cashed in for matter. Smash particles hard enough and brand new ones come out of the wreck, and m = Delta_E/c^2 says how much you get for the energy you paid.
The famous equation, read backwards. m = Delta_E/c^2 takes energy in and hands you mass out. Because c is the speed of light and it gets squared, a huge Delta_E buys only a tiny scrap of m.
Nothing appears for free. Put in energy Delta_E and m = Delta_E/c^2 is the mass you can get out, but conservation of charge and momentum still decides which particles are allowed to appear.
anchor: accelerators aiming a beam at a target and creating new matter in the collision, with conservation laws limiting what can appear

name: Radius of a particle's path in a magnetic field
variants: Fire a charged particle across a magnetic field and it bends into a circle. r = m*v/(q*B). Heavy or fast, it swings wide. More charge or a stronger field, and it curls in tight.
Mass spectrometers weigh atoms by bending them. Hold v, q and B fixed and r = m*v/(q*B) leaves the radius proportional to m, so where the ion lands on the detector tells you its mass.
A track curling in a bubble chamber is not decoration, it is data. r = m*v/(q*B) turns the size of the arc into m*v, and which way it curls tells you the sign of the charge q.
anchor: the mass spectrometer fixing v, q and B so radius reads off mass at the detector, plus curling tracks in a bubble chamber

name: Energy quantum of radiation
variants: Light does not arrive as a smooth stream. It comes in lumps, and Delta_E = h*f is the size of one lump at frequency f. Bluer light hits harder per lump. Brighter light just sends more of them.

Planck found that a hot object sheds energy in whole chunks, never a trickle. Delta_E = h*f gives the size of one chunk, h being Planck's constant. Einstein used it to explain the photoelectric effect.
Picture a car allowed only certain speeds, nothing in between. Energy behaves that way here. Delta_E = h*f is the smallest bite of radiation at frequency f, and you cannot have half a bite.
anchor: the OpenStax car-that-can-only-travel-at-certain-speeds analogy, and Planck's blackbody chunks feeding Einstein's photoelectric effect

name: x component of a vector
variants: A vector pointing off at an angle still gets you somewhere sideways. How much is v_x = v*cos(theta). At theta = 0 it is all sideways; at a right angle the cosine is zero and none of it is.
Shine a light straight down on an arrow and the shadow it casts along the x axis is v_x = v*cos(theta). Tilt the arrow further and the shadow shrinks, which is the cosine doing its job.
v_x = v*cos(theta) splits a vector into the part that acts along x. Past 90 degrees the cosine turns negative, and so does v_x, which is the notation telling you it now points the other way.
anchor: A99 hand-written

name: y component of a vector
variants: The part of a vector that acts upward is v_y = v*sin(theta). At theta = 0 there is none of it, which is why a ball rolled flat along a table never leaves the table.
v_y = v*sin(theta) is the other shadow: how much of v points along y. Sine and cosine split one vector between two axes, and nothing is lost, because their squares add to one.
Launch something at theta and only v_y = v*sin(theta) fights gravity. The sideways part does not, which is why the angle you throw at decides how long it hangs in the air.
anchor: A99 hand-written

name: magnitude of a vector from its components
variants: Two perpendicular components make a right triangle, so the vector itself is the hypotenuse: v = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2). Three sideways and four up is five, not seven.
v = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2) is Pythagoras wearing a physics hat. The squares are why a component pointing backward counts the same as one pointing forward: a magnitude has no direction left in it.
Add the squares, take the root, and you have the size of the whole vector. v = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2) is never negative, whatever signs v_x and v_y carry.
anchor: A99 hand-written

name: direction of a vector from its components
variants: The components tell you which way the vector points: theta = atan(v_y/v_x). It is the ratio that matters, not the size, so doubling both leaves the direction alone.
theta = atan(v_y/v_x) recovers the angle from the two shadows. It answers in the first or fourth quadrant only, so if v_x is negative you add half a turn yourself.
Steeper means more v_y for the same v_x, and theta = atan(v_y/v_x) is how that becomes an angle. A vector straight up has v_x = 0, where the ratio blows up and the angle is a right angle.
anchor: A99 hand-written

name: work done by a force at an angle to the displacement
variants: Only the part of a force that points along the motion does any work: W = F*d*cos(theta). Carry a bag across a room and you do none on it, because you push up and it goes sideways.
W = F*d*cos(theta) is a scalar product. Past a right angle the cosine goes negative and so does the work, which is exactly what friction does to something sliding to a stop.
Push at an angle and you waste some of it. The useful share is cos(theta), so W = F*d*cos(theta), and dragging a sled by a rope held low beats holding the rope high.

name: magnitude of torque from a force at an angle
variants: Push a door at the handle and it swings; push it at the hinge and nothing happens. tau = r*F*sin(theta) says why: distance and force both count, and so does the angle between them.
tau = r*F*sin(theta) keeps only the part of the force perpendicular to r. Push straight along the arm and the sine is zero, so you get no turn at all however hard you shove.
Torque is a vector product, and its size is tau = r*F*sin(theta). Same force further out turns things harder, which is why a long wrench loosens what a short one will not.

name: component of a resultant vector
variants: Vectors add one axis at a time: R_x = A_x + B_x. Walk east then west and the two components cancel, because each carries its own sign.
R_x = A_x + B_x is why vector addition is easy once you break things into components. Do the same along y and you have the whole resultant, with no triangles to draw.
Two forces on one object combine to R_x = A_x + B_x along x. Nothing here is special to force; displacement, velocity and momentum all add the same way.
